subtopic: Currency exchange with commission
statement: A traveler exchanges $1500$ US dollars (USD) into euros (EUR) at a rate of $1$ USD $=0.9210$ EUR. A commission of $2\%$ is then deducted from the euros received. Round every money value to the nearest cent (two decimal places) and use the rounded value in later parts. (a) Find the amount in EUR that the traveler receives after the commission. [2] (b) The traveler spends $1050$ EUR and converts the rest back to USD at a rate of $1$ EUR $=1.0750$ USD with no commission. Find the amount in USD received. [3] (c) A second booth offers $1$ USD $=0.9250$ EUR with a commission of $3.5\%$ on the euros received. Find, to the nearest cent, how many more euros the first booth gives for the original $1500$ USD. [3]
tips: Apply the commission as a multiplier ($1-0.02$). Round only at the stage the question tells you to.

subtopic: Decibels and logarithms
statement: The sound level $L$, in decibels (dB), of a sound of intensity $I$ watts per square meter is given by $L=10\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)$. (a) A conversation has intensity $I=10^{-5}$ W m$^{-2}$. Find its sound level. [2] (b) A rock concert has a sound level of $110$ dB. Find its intensity $I$ in W m$^{-2}$. [3] (c) The level of a sound increases by $20$ dB. Find the factor by which its intensity is multiplied. [2]
markscheme: (a) $L=10\log_{10}\!\left(10^{7}\right)$ [M1]; $L=70$ dB [A1] [2 marks] (b) $110=10\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)\Rightarrow\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}\right)=11$ [M1]; $\dfrac{I}{10^{-12}}=10^{11}$ [A1]; $I=10^{-1}=0.1$ W m$^{-2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) Increase of $20$ dB means $\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1}\right)=2$ [M1]; the intensity is multiplied by $100$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Undo $\log_{10}$ by raising $10$ to both sides. A difference of $10$ dB multiplies the intensity by $10$.

subtopic: Standard form with light-years
statement: Light travels at $3.00\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$. One year is $3.15\times10^{7}$ seconds. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. Give all answers in the form $a\times10^{k}$ where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb Z$. (a) Find the length of one light-year in kilometers. [3] (b) A star is $4.2$ light-years from Earth. Find this distance in kilometers. [2] (c) A probe travels at $2.1\times10^{1}$ km s$^{-1}$. Use the unrounded distance from part (b) to find the time, in years, it takes to reach the star. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3.00\times10^{8}\times3.15\times10^{7}=9.45\times10^{15}$ m [M1][A1]; $9.45\times10^{12}$ km [A1] [3 marks] (b) $4.2\times9.45\times10^{12}$ [M1]; $3.969\times10^{13}$ km, which is $3.97\times10^{13}$ km to 3 significant figures [A1] [2 marks] (c) time in seconds $=\dfrac{3.969\times10^{13}}{21}=1.89\times10^{12}$ s [M1][A1]; $\dfrac{1.89\times10^{12}}{3.15\times10^{7}}=6.0\times10^{4}$ years [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Convert meters to kilometers by dividing by $10^{3}$. Divide coefficients and subtract exponents.

subtopic: Reverse percentages and successive changes
statement: A jacket is reduced by $15\%$ in a sale. A sales tax of $8\%$ is then added to the sale price, and the jacket costs $229.50$ dollars in total. (a) Find the original price of the jacket, before the sale. [3] (b) Find the single percentage change that is equivalent to the reduction followed by the tax. [2] (c) Another shop raises a price by $20\%$ and later lowers the new price by $20\%$. Find the overall percentage change in the price. [2]
markscheme: (a) Multiplier $0.85\times1.08=0.918$ [M1]; $\dfrac{229.50}{0.918}$ [M1]; original price $=250$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $0.918-1=-0.082$ [M1]; a decrease of $8.2\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1.2\times0.8=0.96$ [M1]; an overall decrease of $4\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Percentage changes multiply; they do not add. To reverse one, divide by the multiplier.

subtopic: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
statement: An arithmetic sequence has fourth term $u_4=19$ and ninth term $u_9=44$. (a) Find the common difference $d$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find $S_{20}$, the sum of the first $20$ terms. [2] (c) Given that $u_n=99$, find the value of $n$. [2]
tips: Subtract the two term formulas $u_n=u_1+(n-1)d$ to get $d$ first.

subtopic: Geometric sequence: ratio, threshold and sum
statement: A geometric sequence has second term $u_2=12$ and fifth term $u_5=40.5$. (a) Find the common ratio $r$ and the first term $u_1$. [3] (b) Find the least value of $n$ for which $u_n>1000$. [3] (c) Find $S_{10}$, the sum of the first $10$ terms, correct to 4 significant figures. [2]
tips: Divide the two given terms to isolate $r^{3}$. For the inequality, take logarithms (or use the GDC table).

subtopic: Regular deposits into a savings account
statement: Kofi opens a savings account that pays $4.8\%$ per year, compounded monthly. He deposits $200$ dollars at the end of every month, starting at the end of the first month. Round money to the nearest cent. (a) Find the balance in the account immediately after his $36$th deposit. [3] (b) Find the least number of deposits needed for the balance to exceed $10000$ dollars, immediately after a deposit. [3] (c) Kofi stops making deposits after the $36$th deposit and leaves the balance from part (a) to earn interest, with no further deposits. Find the balance $24$ months later. [2]
markscheme: (a) monthly rate $=\dfrac{4.8}{12}=0.4\%$ [M1]; GDC finance solver with $N=36$, $I\%=4.8$, $PMT=-200$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1]; $FV=7727.62$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) set $FV=10000$ and solve for $N$ [M1]; $N=45.7$ [A1]; the balance first exceeds $10000$ after the $46$th deposit [A1] [3 marks] (c) $7727.62\times\left(1+0.004\right)^{24}$ [M1]; $=8504.62$ dollars [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use $PMT=-200$ (money paid out) and $FV$ positive. Check the integer $N$ either side of the solver output.

subtopic: Loan repaid by monthly payments
statement: A loan of $18000$ dollars is borrowed at $7.2\%$ per year, compounded monthly, and repaid by $36$ equal payments made at the end of each month. (a) Find the monthly payment, to the nearest cent. [3] (b) Using the rounded payment from part (a), find the total interest paid over the $36$ months. [2] (c) Use the unrounded monthly payment to find the amount still owed immediately after the $12$th payment, to the nearest cent. [3]
markscheme: (a) GDC finance solver: $N=36$, $I\%=7.2$, $PV=18000$, $FV=0$, $P/Y=C/Y=12$ [M1][M1]; $PMT=557.44$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $36\times557.44=20067.84$ [M1]; interest $=20067.84-18000=2067.84$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (c) $N=12$ payments made, so find $FV$ of the loan [M1]; with $PMT=-557.4352\ldots$ [A1]; balance $=12425.19$ dollars [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Total interest is total repaid minus the amount borrowed. The balance owed is the future value after $12$ payments.

subtopic: Sum using sigma notation
statement: Let $S_n=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}(3k+2)$. (a) Find $S_{15}$. [2] (b) Show that $S_n=\dfrac{n(3n+7)}{2}$. [3] (c) Given that $S_n=948$, find the value of $n$. [3]
markscheme: (a) arithmetic series with $u_1=5$, $d=3$ [M1]; $S_{15}=\dfrac{15}{2}\left(10+14\times3\right)=390$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times5+(n-1)\times3\right)$ [M1][A1]; $=\dfrac{n(3n+7)}{2}$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $3n^{2}+7n-1896=0$ [M1]; $(n-24)(3n+79)=0$ [A1]; $n=24$ (since $n>0$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Identify the first term and common difference of $3k+2$ before using the sum formula.

subtopic: Geometric sequence with an unknown middle term
statement: The first three terms of a geometric sequence are $4$, $x$ and $36$, where $x>0$. (a) Find the value of $x$ and the common ratio $r$. [3] (b) Find the sum of the first $6$ terms. [2] (c) Find the least value of $n$ for which $u_n>10^{4}$. [3]
tips: In a geometric sequence the ratio of consecutive terms is constant, so $\frac{u_2}{u_1}=\frac{u_3}{u_2}$.

subtopic: Arithmetic model for a training plan
statement: A runner follows a training plan. In week $1$ she runs $5$ km in total, and each week she runs $0.75$ km more than the week before. (a) Find the distance she runs in week $12$. [2] (b) Find the total distance she runs in the first $12$ weeks. [2] (c) Find the least number of weeks after which her total distance run since week $1$ exceeds $300$ km. [3]
tips: Use the sum formula with the GDC, and check the integer values either side of the crossing point.

subtopic: Ticket prices from two simultaneous equations
statement: At a school play, an adult ticket costs $a$ dollars and a student ticket costs $s$ dollars. Three adult tickets and two student tickets cost $41$ dollars in total. Two adult tickets and five student tickets cost $53$ dollars in total. (a) Write down two equations in $a$ and $s$ and solve them to find $a$ and $s$. [4] (b) Find the cost of four adult tickets and three student tickets. [1] (c) A group of $12$ people, each with an adult or a student ticket, pays $102$ dollars in total. Find how many of them hold adult tickets. [3]
markscheme: (a) $3a+2s=41$ and $2a+5s=53$ [A1]; eliminate, e.g. $15a+10s=205$ and $4a+10s=106$ [M1]; $11a=99$ so $a=9$ [A1]; $s=7$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $4\times9+3\times7=57$ dollars [A1] [1 mark] (c) let $x$ adult and $y$ student tickets: $x+y=12$ and $9x+7y=102$ [M1]; $9x+7(12-x)=102$ so $2x=18$ [A1]; $x=9$ adult tickets [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Multiply one or both equations so that a variable has equal coefficients, then add or subtract.

subtopic: Three unknown prices by elimination
statement: In a stationery shop a pen costs $p$ dollars, a notebook costs $n$ dollars and a folder costs $f$ dollars. Three orders are made: $3p+2n+f=19$, $2p+n+2f=15$ and $p+3n+2f=23$. (a) Solve the system of equations to find $p$, $n$ and $f$, showing your elimination steps. [6] (b) Find the total cost of two pens, two notebooks and two folders. [1]
markscheme: (a) eliminate $f$: eq2 $-$ eq3 gives $p-2n=-8$ [M1][A1]; $2\times$eq1 $-$ eq2 gives $4p+3n=23$ [M1][A1]; solving, $p=2$, $n=5$ [A1]; $f=19-6-10=3$ [A1] [6 marks] (b) $2(2+5+3)=20$ dollars [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations to get a $2\times2$ system.

subtopic: Quadratic model of a ball's height
statement: The height $h$ meters of a ball above the ground $t$ seconds after it is thrown is modeled by $h=at^{2}+bt+c$. The height is $10.25$ m when $t=0.5$, $16.5$ m when $t=1$ and $20.25$ m when $t=2.5$. (a) Write down three linear equations in $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (b) Solve the equations using your GDC to find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [2] (c) Find the greatest height of the ball and the time at which it occurs. [3] (d) Find the time at which the ball lands on the ground, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $0.25a+0.5b+c=10.25$ [A1]; $a+b+c=16.5$ and $6.25a+2.5b+c=20.25$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) GDC simultaneous equation solver [M1]; $a=-5$, $b=20$, $c=1.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}=2$ s [M1][A1]; greatest height $h(2)=21.5$ m [A1] [3 marks] (d) solve $-5t^{2}+20t+1.5=0$ [M1]; $t=4.07$ s (reject the negative root) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute each data point into the model to get three equations, then use the GDC. The vertex of a quadratic is at $t=-\frac{b}{2a}$.

subtopic: Mixing three acid solutions
statement: A chemist mixes three solutions containing $10\%$, $20\%$ and $40\%$ acid by volume. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of liters of the $10\%$, $20\%$ and $40\%$ solutions used. The mixture has a total volume of $60$ L and contains $11$ L of pure acid. The volume of the $10\%$ solution is three times the volume of the $40\%$ solution. (a) Write down three linear equations for $x$, $y$ and $z$. [3] (b) Solve the system to find $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (c) Find the percentage concentration of acid in the final mixture, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Each equation comes from a different fact: total volume, total acid, and the stated ratio.

subtopic: Intersecting lines and parameters
statement: Consider the system of equations $x+ky=3$ and $2x+8y=m$, where $k$ and $m$ are constants. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [2] (b) With this value of $k$, find the value of $m$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions. [2] (c) With this value of $k$ and $m=10$, state, with a reason, the number of solutions. [2]
markscheme: (a) unique solution fails when the lines are parallel [M1]; $\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{k}{8}$ so $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $2x+8y=m$ must be $2\times(x+4y=3)$ [M1]; $m=6$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the equations give $x+4y=3$ and $x+4y=5$ [M1]; these are contradictory, so there is no solution (parallel distinct lines) [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Two lines in a plane have no unique intersection when they are parallel: equal gradients.

subtopic: Diet plan with a matrix equation
statement: Three foods X, Y and Z are mixed in portions of $100$ g. Each $100$ g of X, Y and Z contains respectively $20$ g, $8$ g and $2$ g of protein, $5$ g, $30$ g and $60$ g of carbohydrate, and $3$ g, $1$ g and $10$ g of fat. A diet requires $63.6$ g of protein, $105.5$ g of carbohydrate and $17$ g of fat. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of $100$ g portions of X, Y and Z. (a) Write the requirements as a matrix equation $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, stating $A$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. [3] (b) Use your GDC to solve the matrix equation and state the mass in grams of each food needed. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} 20 & 8 & 2 \\ 5 & 30 & 60 \\ 3 & 1 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 63.6 \\ 105.5 \\ 17 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\mathbf{v}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=2.5$, $y=1.5$, $z=0.8$ [A1]; $250$ g of X, $150$ g of Y, $80$ g of Z [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Each row of $A$ is one nutrient and each column is one food. Then $\mathbf{v}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ on the GDC.

subtopic: Investment portfolio
statement: A trust invests $80000$ dollars in bonds, stocks and property. Let $b$, $s$ and $p$ be the amounts, in dollars, invested in bonds, stocks and property. The yearly returns are $3\%$ on bonds, $7\%$ on stocks and $10\%$ on property, and the total return for the year is $4200$ dollars. The amount invested in stocks is twice the amount invested in property. (a) Write down three equations for $b$, $s$ and $p$. [3] (b) Solve the equations to find $b$, $s$ and $p$. [2] (c) The next year the rates fall to $2\%$, $6\%$ and $9\%$ respectively, with the same amounts invested. Find the total return. [2]
tips: Percentages become decimal multipliers in the return equation; the third condition is $s-2p=0$.

subtopic: Rectangle from perimeter and length condition
statement: A rectangle has perimeter $54$ cm. Its length is $3$ cm more than twice its width. (a) Let $w$ be the width and $l$ the length, in cm. Find $w$ and $l$. [3] (b) Find the area of the rectangle. [1] (c) Find the length of a diagonal, giving your answer as a surd in simplest form. [2]
tips: Substitute the length condition into the perimeter equation to get one equation in $w$.

subtopic: Quadratic through three points
statement: A parabola with equation $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$ passes through the points $(0, -2)$, $(2, -2)$ and $(3, 4)$. (a) Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the vertex. [2] (c) Find the exact values of the $x$-intercepts. [2]
tips: Use the point on the $y$-axis first to find $c$, then form two equations in $a$ and $b$.

subtopic: Market equilibrium and a tax
statement: In a market, the price $p$ dollars of a product when $q$ units are demanded is $p=150-0.5q$. The price at which $q$ units are supplied is $p=20+0.8q$. (a) Find the equilibrium quantity and the equilibrium price. [3] (b) A tax of $13$ dollars per unit is introduced, so that the supply equation becomes $p=33+0.8q$. Find the new equilibrium quantity and price. [3] (c) Find the total tax revenue collected, and the increase in the price paid by consumers per unit. [2]
markscheme: (a) $150-0.5q=20+0.8q$ [M1]; $q=100$ [A1]; $p=100$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (b) $150-0.5q=33+0.8q$ [M1]; $q=90$ [A1]; $p=105$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (c) tax revenue $=13\times90=1170$ dollars [A1]; price rise $=105-100=5$ dollars per unit [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Equilibrium is where the demand and supply prices are equal. A per-unit tax shifts the supply line up by the tax.

subtopic: Break-even between two printers
statement: Printer A charges a set-up fee of $80$ dollars plus $0.45$ dollars per copy. Printer B charges a set-up fee of $150$ dollars plus $0.30$ dollars per copy. For $n$ copies, the costs are $C_A$ and $C_B$ dollars. (a) Write down expressions for $C_A$ and $C_B$ in terms of $n$. [2] (b) Find the number of copies for which both printers charge the same, giving your answer to 1 decimal place. [2] (c) Find the least whole number of copies for which printer B is cheaper, and find how much cheaper B is than A for $600$ copies. [3]
tips: The costs are equal where the two lines intersect. Beyond that point the line with the smaller gradient is cheaper.

subtopic: Parameter k in a three-variable system
statement: Consider the system $x+2y+z=4$, $2x+3y+kz=9$ and $x+y+2z=5$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$ for which the system does not have a unique solution. [3] (b) For this value of $k$, show that the system is consistent and find the general solution in terms of a parameter $t=z$. [4] (c) For $k=2$, use your GDC to solve the system. [2]
markscheme: (a) coefficient matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & k \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $k-3$ [M1][A1]; $k=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) subtract eq3 from eq1: $y-z=-1$ so $y=t-1$ [M1][A1]; $x=4-2(t-1)-t=6-3t$ [A1]; sum of eq1 and eq3 gives eq2 (LHS and RHS), so the equations are consistent with infinitely many solutions $(6-3t,\ t-1,\ t)$ [R1] [4 marks] (c) unique solution since $k\ne3$ [M1]; $x=6$, $y=-1$, $z=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A zero determinant means no unique solution. Check consistency by seeing whether the dependent equation's right-hand side matches.

subtopic: Currents in a circuit
statement: Three currents $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$, in amperes, in an electrical circuit satisfy $I_1=I_2+I_3$, $4I_1+6I_2=12$ and $6I_2-3I_3=0$. (a) Show that $I_3=2I_2$ and $I_1=3I_2$. [2] (b) Hence find the three currents. [3]
tips: Reduce to one unknown by writing $I_1$ and $I_3$ in terms of $I_2$.

subtopic: Piecewise quadratic path joined smoothly
statement: This question models the path of a stunt cyclist over a ramp. The height $y$ meters at horizontal distance $x$ meters is given by $y=f(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ for $0\le x\le3$ and by $y=g(x)=px^{2}+qx+r$ for $3\le x\le8$. The first piece passes through $(0, 0)$ and $(3, 3.6)$, and its gradient at $x=3$ is $2.4$. (a) Write down three equations for $a$, $b$ and $c$ and solve them to find $f(x)$. [4] (b) The second piece joins the first at $(3, 3.6)$ with the same gradient there, and passes through $(8, 0.6)$. Write down three equations for $p$, $q$ and $r$. [3] (c) Solve these equations to find $g(x)$. [2] (d) Find the greatest height of the cyclist and the value of $x$ where it occurs. [3] (e) Find the values of $x$, between $3$ and $8$, for which the height is at least $5$ m, to 3 significant figures. [3] (f) State one way in which the model would be unrealistic if the two pieces met at $x=3$ with different gradients. [1]
tips: Continuity gives the point equation and smoothness gives equal gradients, so both pieces share the derivative value at $x=3$.

subtopic: Production planning with three resources
statement: A factory makes three products P, Q and R. One unit of P, Q and R uses respectively $2$, $1$ and $1$ hours of machine time, $1$, $2$ and $1$ hours of labor, and $1$, $1$ and $2$ units of material. In one week, $110$ hours of machine time and $90$ hours of labor are available, and $t$ units of material are available. Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be the numbers of P, Q and R made, using all resources. (a) Write the conditions as a matrix equation $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, giving $M$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Find $\det M$ and explain what this tells you about the solutions for any value of $t$. [2] (c) For $t=100$, find $x$, $y$ and $z$. [2] (d) The profits are $40$, $55$ and $60$ dollars per unit of P, Q and R. Find the total profit for $t=100$. [2] (e) Use $M^{-1}$ to find $x$, $y$ and $z$ in terms of $t$. [3] (f) Find the range of values of $t$ for which $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all non-negative, giving the bounds to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{v}=\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\mathbf{b}=\begin{pmatrix} 110 \\ 90 \\ t \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det M=4$ [A1]; $\det M\neq0$ so $M^{-1}$ exists and there is exactly one solution for every $t$ [R1] [2 marks] (c) $\mathbf{v}=M^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ [M1]; $x=35$, $y=15$, $z=25$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $35\times40+15\times55+25\times60$ [M1]; $3725$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (e) $\mathbf{v}=\dfrac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 110 \\ 90 \\ t \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{240-t}{4}$ [A1]; $y=\dfrac{160-t}{4}$ and $z=\dfrac{3t-200}{4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (f) $x\ge0\Rightarrow t\le240$ and $y\ge0\Rightarrow t\le160$ [M1]; $z\ge0\Rightarrow t\ge\dfrac{200}{3}$ [A1]; $66.7\le t\le160$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Write the system as $M\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$, find $M^{-1}$ with the GDC, and keep $t$ symbolic in the last column of $\mathbf{b}$.

subtopic: Polar and Cartesian forms with products and quotients
statement: Let $z=-3+5i$ and $w=4e^{0.6i}$. Give moduli and arguments correct to 3 significant figures, with arguments in radians in the interval $(-\pi,\pi]$. (a) Find the modulus and the argument of $z$. [3] (b) Find the modulus and argument of $zw$ and of $\dfrac{z}{w}$. [4] (c) Write $w$ in the form $a+bi$, giving $a$ and $b$ to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Multiply moduli and add arguments for a product; divide moduli and subtract arguments for a quotient. Work in radian mode.

subtopic: Quadratic with complex roots in Euler form
statement: Consider the equation $z^{2}-4z+8=0$ where $z\in\mathbb{C}$. (a) Solve the equation, giving the roots in the form $a+bi$. [3] (b) Write the root with positive imaginary part in the form $re^{i\theta}$, where $r>0$ and $\theta$ is exact. [3] (c) Write down the other root in the form $re^{i\theta}$, and state the sum of the two roots. [2]
markscheme: (a) $z=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16-32}}{2}$ [M1]; $\sqrt{-16}=4i$ [A1]; $z=2\pm2i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $r=\sqrt{4+4}=2\sqrt2$ [A1]; $\theta=\arctan\dfrac{2}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ [M1]; $2\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2\sqrt2e^{-i\pi/4}$ [A1]; sum $=4$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Complex roots of a real quadratic come in conjugate pairs, so the second root has the same modulus and the negative argument.

subtopic: Exact product and quotient in Euler form
statement: Let $z=-2+2\sqrt3\,i$ and $w=2e^{i\pi/6}$. (a) Find $|z|$ and $\arg z$ exactly, and write $z$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$. [3] (b) Find $zw$ in the form $re^{i\theta}$ and then in the form $a+bi$ with exact values. [3] (c) Find $\dfrac{z}{w}$ in the form $a+bi$. [2]
tips: Use $\tan\theta=\sqrt3$ for the reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$, then place it in the correct quadrant.

subtopic: Equation involving a complex conjugate
statement: Let $z=a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $z^{*}$ be its complex conjugate. It is given that $z+2z^{*}=9-4i$. (a) Find $a$ and $b$. [3] (b) Find $|z|$, and write down an expression for $\arg z$ in radians. [2] (c) Find $z\,z^{*}$ and hence state the value of $\dfrac{1}{z}$ in the form $c+di$. [2]
tips: Substitute $z=a+bi$ and $z^{*}=a-bi$, then equate real and imaginary parts.

subtopic: Square on the Argand diagram
statement: In the complex plane, the points $A$ and $B$ represent the complex numbers $1+i$ and $5+3i$. Multiplying a complex number by $i$ rotates it by $90^{\circ}$ anticlockwise about the origin. The points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are the vertices of a square in that order, going anticlockwise. (a) Find $B-A$, and hence find the complex number represented by $C$. [3] (b) Find the complex number represented by $D$, and the area of the square. [3] (c) Find the complex number at the center of the square and the radius of the circle passing through all four vertices. [2]
markscheme: (a) $B-A=4+2i$ [A1]; $C=B+i(B-A)$ [M1]; $C=5+3i+4i-2=3+7i$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $D=A+i(B-A)=1+i+4i-2=-1+5i$ [A1]; side length $\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}$ [M1]; area $=20$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) center $=\dfrac{A+C}{2}=2+4i$ [A1]; radius $=\dfrac{\sqrt{20}\,\sqrt2}{2}=\sqrt{10}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Going around a square anticlockwise, each side vector is the previous one multiplied by $i$.

subtopic: Matrix products, inverse and a singular sum
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find $AB$. [2] (b) Find $A^{-1}$ and hence solve $A\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$. [3] (c) Find the values of $k$ for which $A+kB$ is singular. Give your answers in exact form. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 2+4 & -1 \\ 3+8 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $AB=\begin{pmatrix} 6 & -1 \\ 11 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\det A=1$, $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $x=2$, $y=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $A+kB=\begin{pmatrix} 2+k & 1 \\ 3+4k & 2-k \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\det=(2+k)(2-k)-(3+4k)=1-4k-k^{2}=0$ [M1]; $k=-2\pm\sqrt5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A matrix is singular when its determinant is zero. Expand $(2+k)(2-k)$ carefully.

subtopic: Three-state Markov chain for weather
statement: The weather each day is Sunny (S), Cloudy (C) or Rainy (R). The transition matrix $T$ below gives the probability of moving from the state in the row to the state in the column, in the order S, C, R, from one day to the next. $$T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$$ (a) Today is Sunny. Find the probability that it is Rainy in two days' time. [3] (b) Find the steady state probabilities of S, C and R, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) In a year of $365$ days, estimate the number of rainy days, to the nearest day, assuming the chain has reached its steady state. [2] (d) State one reason why a Markov chain might not be a good model of real weather. [1]
markscheme: (a) required entry of $T^{2}$ [M1]; $0.6\times0.1+0.3\times0.3+0.1\times0.5$ [A1]; $=0.2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) solve $\pi T=\pi$ with $\pi_S+\pi_C+\pi_R=1$ [M1]; $\pi_S=\dfrac{13}{46}=0.283$ [A1]; $\pi_C=0.413$ and $\pi_R=0.304$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $365\times\dfrac{14}{46}$ [M1]; $111$ days [A1] [2 marks] (d) e.g. tomorrow's weather depends on more than today's weather, or the probabilities change with season [R1] [1 mark]
tips: The steady state is the left eigenvector for eigenvalue $1$, normalized so the entries sum to $1$.

subtopic: Diagonalization of a 2 by 2 matrix
statement: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (b) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [2] (c) Write $A=PDP^{-1}$, stating $P$ and $D$, and use it to find $A^{3}$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\det(A-\lambda I)=(4-\lambda)(3-\lambda)-2$ [M1]; $\lambda^{2}-7\lambda+10=0$ [A1]; $\lambda=5$ and $\lambda=2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\lambda=5$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\lambda=2$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $D=\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{3}=PD^{3}P^{-1}$ [M1]; $P^{-1}=-\dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $A^{3}=\begin{pmatrix} 86 & 39 \\ 78 & 47 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Eigenvalues come from $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. Then $A^{n}=PD^{n}P^{-1}$, where the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors.

subtopic: Two-state Markov chain and its eigenvalues
statement: Each day a commuter either drives (D) or cycles (C). The transition matrix, with rows and columns in the order D, C, is $T=\begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$, where each entry is the probability of moving from the row state to the column state. (a) Show that $1$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ and find the other eigenvalue. [3] (b) Find the steady state probability vector. [3] (c) Explain why $T^{n}$ approaches a matrix with identical rows as $n\to\infty$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\lambda^{2}-1.7\lambda+0.7=0$ [M1]; $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-0.7)=0$ [A1]; eigenvalues $1$ and $0.7$ [AG] [3 marks] (b) $\pi=(p,q)$ with $0.9p+0.2q=p$ [M1]; $p=2q$ with $p+q=1$ [A1]; $\pi=\left(\dfrac{2}{3},\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) the eigenvalue $0.7$ has $0.7^{n}\to0$ [R1]; only the eigenvalue $1$ component remains, which gives $\left(\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}\right)$ in every row [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A steady state is a vector $\pi$ with $\pi T=\pi$ whose entries sum to $1$.

subtopic: Sales, prices and profit with matrices
statement: A company sells three products in three towns. The matrix $S$ gives the numbers of units sold, with rows for the towns (Alder, Birch, Cedar) and columns for the products (X, Y, Z): $S=\begin{pmatrix} 120 & 80 & 45 \\ 95 & 110 & 60 \\ 150 & 70 & 30 \end{pmatrix}$. The selling prices in dollars are $4.50$, $7.25$ and $12$ per unit of X, Y and Z. The costs in dollars are $2.80$, $4.90$ and $8.30$ per unit of X, Y and Z. (a) Write the selling prices as a column matrix $\mathbf{p}$ and find $S\mathbf{p}$. State what each entry of $S\mathbf{p}$ represents. [3] (b) Find the total profit from all three towns. [3] (c) The prices of all three products are reduced by $10\%$ with the costs and the numbers sold unchanged. Find the new total profit. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 4.5 \\ 7.25 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $S\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix} 1660 \\ 1945 \\ 1542.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; each entry is the total revenue, in dollars, from one town [A1] [3 marks] (b) profit per unit is $\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{c}$ with $\mathbf{c}=(2.8, 4.9, 8.3)^{T}$ [M1]; $S(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{c})=\begin{pmatrix} 558.5 \\ 642 \\ 530.5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; total $=1731$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (c) new prices $0.9\mathbf{p}$ [M1]; total profit $=1216.25$ dollars [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Rows of $S$ are towns, so $S\mathbf{p}$ gives one revenue per town. Profit per unit is price minus cost.

subtopic: Reflection and enlargement combined
statement: Let $R$ be the reflection in the line $y=-x$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, and let $E$ be the enlargement with center the origin and scale factor $3$. The transformation $M$ is $R$ followed by $E$. (a) Find the matrix of $M$, and the image of the point $P(2, -1)$ under $M$. [3] (b) A triangle has area $4$ square units. Find the area of its image under $M$. [2] (c) Find the coordinates of the point whose image under $M$ is $(6, -12)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $M=\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1]; image of $P$ is $(3, -6)$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\det M=-9$ [A1]; area $=9\times4=36$ square units [A1] [2 marks] (c) $M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\frac13 \\ -\frac13 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; the point is $(4, -2)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For the combined transformation $R$ then $E$, multiply in the order $ER$. The area scale factor is $|\det M|$.

subtopic: Stretch of a circle into an ellipse
statement: A stretch with scale factor $3$ parallel to the $x$-axis and scale factor $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis is applied to the circle $C$ with equation $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$. The image of $C$ is the curve $C'$. (a) Write down the matrix of the transformation. [1] (b) A point $(x, y)$ on $C$ maps to $(X, Y)$. Find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $X$ and $Y$, and hence find the equation of $C'$. [3] (c) The area of $C$ is $\pi$. Find the area enclosed by $C'$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $X=3x$, $Y=2y$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{X}{3}$ and $y=\dfrac{Y}{2}$ [A1]; $\dfrac{X^{2}}{9}+\dfrac{Y^{2}}{4}=1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\det=6$ [M1]; area $=6\pi$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Substitute $x=X/3$ and $y=Y/2$ into the original equation to get the image curve.

subtopic: Rotation and enlargement using a GDC
statement: Let $R$ be the rotation of $35^{\circ}$ anticlockwise about the origin and let $E$ be the enlargement with center the origin and scale factor $2.5$. Let $M$ be the transformation $R$ followed by $E$. (a) Write down the matrix of $R$, with entries correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find the image of the point $A(4, 1)$ under $M$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) A triangle of area $6$ square units is transformed by $M$. Find the area of its image. [2] (d) Use $M^{-1}$ to find the point whose image under $M$ is $(10, 5)$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\begin{pmatrix} \cos35^{\circ} & -\sin35^{\circ} \\ \sin35^{\circ} & \cos35^{\circ} \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\begin{pmatrix} 0.819 & -0.574 \\ 0.574 & 0.819 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) matrix of $M$ is $2.5R$ [M1]; $M\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $(6.76, 7.78)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\det M=2.5^{2}=6.25$ [A1]; $6\times6.25=37.5$ square units [A1] [2 marks] (d) $M^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 10 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $(4.42, -0.656)$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use degree mode for $\cos35^{\circ}$. To apply $R$ then $E$, premultiply by the matrices in the order $ER$.

subtopic: Line in three dimensions: points and perpendicular direction
statement: A line $L$ has equation $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the coordinates of the point on $L$ where $t=3$. [1] (b) Determine whether the point $Q(9, -2, 11)$ lies on $L$. [3] (c) Find the value of $k$ such that $\begin{pmatrix} k \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ is perpendicular to the direction of $L$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $(7, -1, 8)$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $1+2t=9$ gives $t=4$ [M1]; $2-t=-2$ gives $t=4$ and $-1+3t=11$ gives $t=4$ [A1]; the same $t$ works, so $Q$ lies on $L$ [R1] [3 marks] (c) scalar product $=0$ [M1]; $2k-2-3=0$ [A1]; $k=\dfrac{5}{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Equate each coordinate to the same parameter value; perpendicular vectors have scalar product zero.

subtopic: Intersection and angle between two lines
statement: Two lines have equations $L_1:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $L_2:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$. (a) Show that $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect and find the coordinates of the point of intersection. [4] (b) Find the acute angle between the lines, correct to 1 decimal place. [4]
markscheme: (a) $1+s=5-2t$ and $2s=3+t$ [M1]; solving, $s=2$, $t=1$ [A1]; third coordinate: $2-2=0$ and $-4+4=0$, so consistent [R1]; point $(3, 4, 0)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) direction scalar product $=-2+2-4=-4$ [A1]; $|d_1|=\sqrt6$ and $|d_2|=\sqrt{21}$ [A1]; $\cos\theta=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{126}}$ (acute angle uses the absolute value) [M1]; $\theta=69.1^{\circ}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: If the two parameter values from two coordinates also satisfy the third coordinate, the lines meet. Use $|\cos\theta|$ for the acute angle.

subtopic: Closest approach of two aircraft
statement: Two aircraft $A$ and $B$ have position vectors, in kilometers relative to an airport, $\mathbf{r}_A=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{r}_B=\begin{pmatrix} 20 \\ 1 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$, where $t$ is the time in hours after noon. (a) Find the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$ at time $t$, and show that the square of the distance between the aircraft is $d^{2}=67t^{2}-312t+392$. [3] (b) Find the time at which the aircraft are closest and the minimum distance between them, in kilometers to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Safety rules require a separation of at least $6.5$ km. Find the time interval, in hours to 3 significant figures, during which the aircraft are closer than $6.5$ km. [3]
tips: Work with $d^{2}$ rather than $d$ to avoid the square root, then take the square root of the minimum.

subtopic: Boat with constant velocity
statement: A boat moves with constant velocity $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$. At noon its position vector relative to a harbor $H$ is $\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$ km, where the unit vectors point east and north. (a) Find the speed of the boat. [2] (b) Write down the position vector of the boat $t$ hours after noon, and find its position at $t=3$. [3] (c) Find the time after noon when the boat is due north of the harbor, and its distance from $H$ then. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}$ [M1]; $5$ km h$^{-1}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix} -6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; at $t=3$: $\begin{pmatrix} -6+9 \\ -2+12 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $(3, 10)$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) east coordinate $=0$: $-6+3t=0$ [M1]; $t=2$ hours after noon [A1]; north coordinate $-2+8=6$, so the distance from $H$ is $6$ km [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Due north or south of $H$ means the east coordinate is zero.

subtopic: Triangle in three dimensions: angle and area
statement: The points $A(2, -1, 3)$, $B(4, 1, 3)$ and $C(4, -1, 5)$ are the vertices of a triangle. (a) Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. [2] (b) Find the size of angle $BAC$. [3] (c) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the point $D$ such that $ABDC$ is a parallelogram. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=4$ [A1]; $\cos A=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt8\sqrt8}=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $A=60^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\dfrac12\sqrt8\sqrt8\sin60^{\circ}$ [M1]; $2\sqrt3$ square units [A1] [2 marks] (d) $D=B+\overrightarrow{AC}=(6, 1, 5)$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Angle at $A$ uses the two vectors that start at $A$.

subtopic: Line through two points and a perpendicular line
statement: The points $A(2, -3)$ and $B(6, 5)$ lie on a line $L_1$. (a) Find the gradient of $L_1$ and its equation in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) The line $L_2$ is perpendicular to $L_1$ and passes through $P(1, 4)$. Find its equation in the form $ax+by=d$ with integer coefficients. [3] (c) Find the coordinates of the point where $L_1$ and $L_2$ intersect. [3]
tips: Perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$. Substitute $y=2x-7$ into the second equation to intersect.

subtopic: Piecewise linear electricity tariff
statement: An electricity company charges a fixed fee of $9.50$ dollars per month plus $0.14$ dollars per unit for the first $120$ units used, and $0.21$ dollars per unit for every unit above $120$. Let $C$ dollars be the monthly bill for $u$ units. Round money to the nearest cent. (a) Find the bill for a month in which $95$ units are used, and for a month in which $200$ units are used. [3] (b) Show that, for $u>120$, $C=0.21u+1.1$. [2] (c) A customer's bill must not exceed $61.40$ dollars. Find the greatest whole number of units that can be used. [3]
tips: Remember the two rates apply to different portions of the units used.

subtopic: Temperature conversion function
statement: The temperature in degrees Fahrenheit $F$ is related to the temperature in degrees Celsius $C$ by $F=1.8C+32$. (a) Find the value of $F$ when water boils at $C=100$. [1] (b) Find the value of $C$ when $F=50$. [2] (c) Find the temperature at which $F$ and $C$ have the same numerical value. [2] (d) Write $C$ in terms of $F$. [2]
tips: Set $F=C=x$ to find where the two scales agree.

subtopic: A runner and a cyclist
statement: A runner leaves a town at time $t=0$ hours and runs along a straight road at a constant speed of $8$ km h$^{-1}$. A cyclist leaves the same town $0.6$ hours later and follows the same road at a constant speed of $20$ km h$^{-1}$. Let $d$ km be the distance of each from the town after $t$ hours. (a) Write down $d$ in terms of $t$ for the runner, and for the cyclist when $t\ge0.6$. [2] (b) Find the time at which the cyclist catches the runner and the distance from the town at that time. [3] (c) Find the time, in minutes after the cyclist starts, at which the cyclist is $4$ km ahead of the runner. [3]
markscheme: (a) runner: $d=8t$ [A1]; cyclist: $d=20(t-0.6)$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $8t=20t-12$ [M1]; $t=1$ hour [A1]; $d=8$ km [A1] [3 marks] (c) $20(t-0.6)-8t=4$ [M1]; $t=\dfrac43$ hours [A1]; $\dfrac43-0.6=0.7333$ hours, which is $44$ minutes after the cyclist starts [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The cyclist's distance is zero until $t=0.6$, so use $t-0.6$ for the time spent cycling.

subtopic: Fitting a power model
statement: The mass $W$ kilograms of a fish of length $L$ decimeters is modeled by $W=kL^{n}$. A fish of length $4$ decimeters has mass $6.4$ kg and a fish of length $9$ decimeters has mass $48.6$ kg. (a) Find the value of $n$ and the value of $k$. [4] (b) Use the model to estimate the mass of a fish of length $6$ decimeters, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the length of a fish with mass $100$ kg, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Divide the two equations to eliminate $k$, then take logarithms to find $n$.

subtopic: Exponential decay of a drug
statement: The concentration $C$ mg per liter of a drug in the blood $t$ hours after an injection is modeled by $C=C_0e^{-kt}$, where $C_0$ and $k$ are positive constants. The initial concentration is $100$ mg per liter, and after $3$ hours the concentration is $62$ mg per liter. (a) Write down $C_0$ and find $k$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the time at which the concentration falls to $10$ mg per liter, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the time taken for the concentration to halve, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Use the unrounded value of $k$ in later parts to avoid rounding errors.

subtopic: Arch bridge as a quadratic function
statement: The height $h$ meters of an arch above the water, at a horizontal distance $x$ meters from the left end of its base, is modeled by $h=18-0.02(x-30)^{2}$, for $x$ from $0$ to $60$. (a) Write down the greatest height of the arch and the value of $x$ at which it occurs. [2] (b) Find the height of the arch at $x=10$. [2] (c) Find the values of $x$ for which $h=0$, and hence the width of the arch at water level. [2] (d) Find the exact values of $x$ for which $h=14$. [2]
tips: Vertex form $a(x-p)^{2}+q$ shows the maximum $q$ at $x=p$ directly.

subtopic: Logistic model of a population
statement: The number of fish $N$ in a pond $t$ months after it is stocked is modeled by $N=\dfrac{500}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}$. (a) Find the number of fish at the start, and state the limiting value of $N$ as $t$ increases. [3] (b) Find the time at which there are $400$ fish, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the time at which the population is half of its limiting value, and state what you notice about the graph of $N$ at this time. [3]
markscheme: (a) $N(0)=\dfrac{500}{10}=50$ [A1]; as $t\to\infty$, $e^{-0.5t}\to0$ [M1]; $N\to500$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) solve $\dfrac{500}{1+9e^{-0.5t}}=400$ [M1]; $t=7.17$ months [A1] [2 marks] (c) $N=250$: solve $1+9e^{-0.5t}=2$ [M1]; $t=\dfrac{\ln9}{0.5}=4.39$ months [A1]; the graph is steepest here (the population grows fastest) [R1] [3 marks]
tips: A logistic curve is steepest when $N$ is half the limiting value.

subtopic: Average cost and its minimum
statement: A factory's average cost per unit, in dollars, of producing $n$ units in a day is $C(n)=\dfrac{2000}{n}+4+0.01n$, for $n>0$. (a) Find the average cost per unit when $n=100$. [2] (b) Use your GDC to find the number of units that minimizes the average cost, to the nearest whole number, and the minimum average cost, to the nearest cent. [3] (c) The factory wants the average cost to be at most $15$ dollars. Find the possible whole-number values of $n$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{2000}{100}+4+1$ [M1]; $25$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (b) minimum of $C(n)$ on the GDC [M1]; $n=447$ [A1]; $C=12.94$ dollars [A1] [3 marks] (c) solve $C(n)=15$ [M1]; $n=229.8$ and $n=870.2$ [A1]; $230\le n\le870$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Graph $C(n)$ and use the GDC minimum function. For an inequality, find the intersections with the line $C=15$ first.

subtopic: Composite and inverse of a square-root function
statement: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}$ for $x\ge1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+2$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and state its domain. [2] (b) Find $(g\circ f)(x)$ and state its domain. [2] (c) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3]
markscheme: (a) $f(g(x))=\sqrt{x^{2}+2-1}=\sqrt{x^{2}+1}$ [A1]; domain $x\in\mathbb{R}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $g(f(x))=\left(\sqrt{x-1}\right)^{2}+2=x+1$ [A1]; domain $x\ge1$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $y=\sqrt{x-1}\Rightarrow x=y^{2}+1$ [M1]; $f^{-1}(x)=x^{2}+1$ [A1]; domain $x\ge0$ (the range of $f$) [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The domain of a composite is limited by the inner function's range being inside the outer function's domain.

subtopic: Exponential function: range, inverse and fixed points
statement: Let $f(x)=2e^{x}-3$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$. (a) Write down the range of $f$ and the equation of its horizontal asymptote. [2] (b) Find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state its domain. [3] (c) Solve $f(x)=10$, giving the exact value of $x$. [2] (d) Find the $x$-coordinates of the points where the graphs of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ intersect, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) range $f(x)>-3$ [A1]; asymptote $y=-3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $x=2e^{y}-3\Rightarrow e^{y}=\dfrac{x+3}{2}$ [M1]; $f^{-1}(x)=\ln\!\left(\dfrac{x+3}{2}\right)$ [A1]; domain $x>-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $2e^{x}=13$ [M1]; $x=\ln6.5$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) intersections of $f$ and $f^{-1}$ lie on $y=x$ [R1]; solve $2e^{x}-3=x$ [M1]; $x=-2.89$ and $x=0.583$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: A function and its inverse are reflections in $y=x$, so crossing points of the two graphs lie on $y=x$.

subtopic: Quadratic with a parameter and a restricted inverse
statement: Let $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+k$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Write $f(x)$ in the form $(x-p)^{2}+q$, giving $p$ and $q$ in terms of $k$ where needed. [2] (b) Find the value of $k$ for which the equation $f(x)=0$ has exactly one solution. [2] (c) Now let $k=1$ and consider $f$ on the domain $x\ge2$. Find the range of $f$, and find $f^{-1}(x)$. [4]
markscheme: (a) $(x-2)^{2}-4+k$ [M1]; $p=2$ and $q=k-4$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) discriminant $16-4k=0$ [M1]; $k=4$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $f(x)=(x-2)^{2}-3$ [A1]; range $f(x)\ge-3$ [A1]; $x-2=\sqrt{y+3}$ (positive root since $x\ge2$) [M1]; $f^{-1}(x)=2+\sqrt{x+3}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: The vertex of $(x-p)^{2}+q$ is $(p, q)$; a restricted domain on one side of the vertex makes the function one-to-one.

subtopic: Transforming a parabola in vertex form
statement: The graph of $y=x^{2}$ is transformed to the graph of $y=-3(x+2)^{2}+5$. (a) Describe the sequence of transformations. [3] (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertex and the range of the new function. [2] (c) Find the $y$-intercept of the new graph. [1]
markscheme: (a) translation $\begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; vertical stretch with scale factor $3$ [A1]; reflection in the $x$-axis, then translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) vertex $(-2, 5)$ [A1]; range $y\le5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-3(4)+5=-7$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Read the transformations from the inside out: the bracket moves the graph left or right, outer factors stretch, outer constants move it up or down.

subtopic: Reflected and stretched exponential
statement: The graph of $y=e^{x}$ is transformed to the graph of $y=-2e^{x}+5$. (a) Describe the three transformations that map $y=e^{x}$ to $y=-2e^{x}+5$. [3] (b) Write down the equation of the horizontal asymptote and the range of the new function. [2] (c) Find the exact $x$-intercept. [2]
markscheme: (a) vertical stretch scale factor $2$ [A1]; reflection in the $x$-axis [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) asymptote $y=5$ [A1]; range $y<5$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $-2e^{x}+5=0$ [M1]; $x=\ln\dfrac52$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The asymptote $y=0$ of $e^{x}$ is moved only by the vertical translation.

subtopic: Logarithmic function with a horizontal stretch and shift
statement: Let $f(x)=\ln x$ and $g(x)=\ln(3x-6)+1$. (a) Write $g(x)$ in the form $\ln(x-2)+c$, giving the exact value of $c$, and describe the transformation from $f$ to $g$. [3] (b) State the domain of $g$ and the equation of its vertical asymptote. [2] (c) Find the exact solution of $g(x)=3$ and the $x$-intercept of $g$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) $g(x)=\ln3+\ln(x-2)+1$ [M1]; $c=1+\ln3$ [A1]; translation $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1+\ln3 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) domain $x>2$ [A1]; asymptote $x=2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $3x-6=e^{2}$ [M1]; $x=\dfrac{6+e^{2}}{3}$ [A1]; $x$-intercept: $3x-6=e^{-1}$ gives $x=2.12$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use $\ln(ab)=\ln a+\ln b$ to separate the factor $3$ from $(x-2)$.

subtopic: Reciprocal function in transformed form
statement: The graph of $y=\dfrac1x$ is transformed to the graph of $y=g(x)$ where $g(x)=\dfrac{2x+1}{x-1}$. (a) Show that $g(x)=2+\dfrac{3}{x-1}$. [2] (b) Describe the transformations from $y=\dfrac1x$ to $y=g(x)$. [3] (c) Write down the equations of the asymptotes and find the axes intercepts of the graph of $g$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $2x+1=2(x-1)+3$ [M1]; $g(x)=2+\dfrac{3}{x-1}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) vertical stretch scale factor $3$ [A1]; translation $1$ unit to the right [A1]; translation $2$ units up [A1] [3 marks] (c) asymptotes $x=1$ and $y=2$ [A1]; $x$-intercept $\left(-\dfrac12, 0\right)$ [A1]; $y$-intercept $(0, -1)$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Divide the numerator by $x-1$ to reveal the stretch and translations.

subtopic: Ships leaving a port: cosine rule and bearing
statement: Two ships leave a port $P$ at the same time. Ship $A$ sails on a bearing of $040^{\circ}$ at $15$ km h$^{-1}$ and ship $B$ sails on a bearing of $100^{\circ}$ at $12$ km h$^{-1}$. Both sail in straight lines for $3$ hours. (a) Find the distance $AB$ between the ships after $3$ hours, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (b) Find the size of angle $PAB$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the bearing of ship $B$ from ship $A$, correct to the nearest degree. [2]
markscheme: (a) $PA=45$ and $PB=36$ [A1]; angle $APB=60^{\circ}$ [A1]; $AB^{2}=45^{2}+36^{2}-2(45)(36)\cos60^{\circ}$ [M1]; $AB=41.2$ km [A1] [4 marks] (b) $\dfrac{\sin PAB}{36}=\dfrac{\sin60^{\circ}}{41.243}$ [M1]; $PAB=49.1^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) bearing of $P$ from $A$ is $220^{\circ}$ [A1]; bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $220-49.1=171^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Draw a diagram with north lines at $P$ and $A$. Angle $APB$ is the difference of the two bearings from $P$.

subtopic: Sector and segment of a circle
statement: A sector $OAB$ of a circle with center $O$ and radius $9$ cm has angle $AOB=1.4$ radians. (a) Find the length of arc $AB$ and the area of the sector. [3] (b) Find the area of triangle $OAB$ and hence the area of the segment cut off by chord $AB$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the perimeter of the segment, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) arc $=9\times1.4=12.6$ cm [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times81\times1.4$ [M1]; $56.7$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times81\sin1.4=39.9$ cm$^{2}$ [A1]; segment $=56.7-39.9$ [M1]; $16.8$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) chord $AB=2\times9\sin0.7=11.6$ cm [M1]; perimeter $=12.6+11.6=24.2$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Calculators must be in radian mode. Segment area is sector area minus triangle area.

subtopic: Exact sector, triangle and segment
statement: A sector $OAB$ of a circle with center $O$ and radius $6$ cm has angle $AOB=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$. (a) Find the exact length of arc $AB$ and the exact area of the sector. [3] (b) Find the exact area of triangle $OAB$. [2] (c) Hence write down the exact area of the segment cut off by chord $AB$. [1]
markscheme: (a) arc $=6\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=4\pi$ cm [A1]; area $=\dfrac12\times36\times\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1]; $12\pi$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times36\times\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ [M1]; $9\sqrt3$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $12\pi-9\sqrt3$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Use $\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ from the special triangle.

subtopic: Triangle from two sides and the area
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=7$ cm, $BC=10$ cm and the area of the triangle is $28$ cm$^{2}$. Angle $ABC$ is $\theta$. (a) Find $\sin\theta$. [2] (b) Find the two possible sizes of $\theta$ in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place. [2] (c) For each value of $\theta$, find the length of $AC$, correct to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac12\times7\times10\sin\theta=28$ [M1]; $\sin\theta=0.8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $\theta=53.1^{\circ}$ [A1]; $\theta=180-53.1=126.9^{\circ}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $AC^{2}=49+100-140\cos\theta$ [M1]; for $\theta=53.1^{\circ}$, $\cos\theta=0.6$ and $AC^{2}=65$ [A1]; $AC=8.06$ cm [A1]; for $\theta=126.9^{\circ}$, $AC^{2}=233$ so $AC=15.3$ cm [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Two sides and the area give $\sin\theta$; both an acute and an obtuse angle have that sine.

subtopic: Height of a tower from two angles of elevation
statement: A vertical tower $TB$ stands on level ground, with $B$ at the base. From a point $P$ on the ground, the angle of elevation of the top $T$ is $25^{\circ}$. From a point $Q$, $40$ m closer to the tower on the same straight line through $B$, the angle of elevation of $T$ is $38^{\circ}$. (a) Write expressions for $PB$ and $QB$ in terms of the height $h$ of the tower. [2] (b) Find $h$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the distance $PB$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) $PB=\dfrac{h}{\tan25^{\circ}}$ [A1]; $QB=\dfrac{h}{\tan38^{\circ}}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $PB-QB=40$ [M1]; $h\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan25^{\circ}}-\dfrac{1}{\tan38^{\circ}}\right)=40$ [A1]; $h=46.3$ m [A1] [3 marks] (c) $PB=\dfrac{46.27}{\tan25^{\circ}}$ [M1]; $99.2$ m [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Both distances to the base involve the same height, and their difference is $40$ m.

subtopic: Triangle with an angle of 120 degrees
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB=3$ cm, $AC=5$ cm and $BC=7$ cm. (a) Use the cosine rule to find angle $BAC$. [3] (b) Find the exact area of the triangle. [2] (c) Find the exact shortest distance from $A$ to the line $BC$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\cos A=\dfrac{3^{2}+5^{2}-7^{2}}{2\times3\times5}$ [M1]; $=-\dfrac12$ [A1]; $A=120^{\circ}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\dfrac12\times3\times5\times\sin120^{\circ}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{15\sqrt3}{4}$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) area $=\dfrac12\times7\times h$ [M1]; $h=\dfrac{15\sqrt3}{14}$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Area equals half base times height, so equate the two expressions for the area to find the perpendicular height.

subtopic: Daylight hours as a sinusoidal model
statement: The number of hours of daylight $D$ in a town is modeled by $D(t)=a\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}(t-c)\right)+d$, where $t$ is the time in months after January $1$ and $a$, $c$, $d$ are positive constants. The greatest number of daylight hours is $15.6$, at $t=6.5$, and the least is $8.4$. (a) Find $a$ and $d$. [3] (b) Find the smallest positive value of $c$. [2] (c) Find the number of hours of daylight at $t=3$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the values of $t$, between $0$ and $12$, for which there are more than $14$ hours of daylight, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Amplitude is half the range, the midline is the mean of the extremes, and the maximum of $\sin$ occurs when the bracket equals $\frac{\pi}{2}$.

subtopic: Solving an equation for a cosine transformation
statement: Let $f(x)=3\cos(2x)-1$ for $0\le x\le\pi$. (a) Write down the amplitude, the period and the range of $f$. [3] (b) Find the exact solutions of $f(x)=\dfrac12$. [4]
markscheme: (a) amplitude $3$ [A1]; period $\pi$ [A1]; range $-4\le f(x)\le2$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $3\cos2x=\dfrac32$ so $\cos2x=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $2x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ [A1][A1]; $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Solve for $\cos2x$ first, then list every value of $2x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ before halving.

subtopic: Mass on a spring
statement: The height $h$ cm above a table of a mass hanging on a spring is modeled by $h=20-6\cos(2.5\pi t)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds after the mass is released. (a) Write down the greatest and the least heights, and the period of the motion. [3] (b) Find the height at $t=0.15$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the first time the height is $22$ cm, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the total time in the first $4$ seconds for which the height is greater than $22$ cm, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) greatest $26$ cm and least $14$ cm [A1][A1]; period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{2.5\pi}=0.8$ s [A1] [3 marks] (b) $20-6\cos(0.375\pi)$ [M1]; $17.7$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\cos(2.5\pi t)=-\dfrac13$ [M1]; $t=0.243$ s [A1] [2 marks] (d) in one period the height is above $22$ for $\dfrac{2\pi-2\arccos(-1/3)}{2\pi}\times0.8=0.313$ s [M1][A1]; there are $5$ periods in $4$ s, so total $=1.57$ s [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use radian mode. Over each full period the time above a level is the same, so multiply by the number of periods.

subtopic: Sinusoidal function from its extremes
statement: The function $f(x)=a\sin(bx)+c$, where $a, b>0$, has period $\pi$, maximum value $7$ and minimum value $-1$. (a) Find $a$, $b$ and $c$. [3] (b) Find the exact value of $f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right)$. [2] (c) Find the exact solutions of $f(x)=5$ for $0\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $b=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$ [A1]; $a=\dfrac{7-(-1)}{2}=4$ [A1]; $c=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $4\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}+3$ [M1]; $2\sqrt2+3$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $\sin2x=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $2x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ [A1]; $x=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Period $=\frac{2\pi}{b}$; the midline is the average of the maximum and minimum.

subtopic: Right triangular prism: lengths, angle and area
statement: A solid right prism has a right-angled triangular base $ABC$ with the right angle at $B$, $AB=6$ cm and $BC=8$ cm. The vertical edges $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ each have length $12$ cm, with $D$, $E$ and $F$ above $A$, $B$ and $C$. (a) Find the length of $AC$, and the volume of the prism. [3] (b) Find the length of $CD$, correct to 3 significant figures, and the angle that $CD$ makes with the base $ABC$, correct to the nearest degree. [4] (c) Find the total surface area of the prism. [2]
markscheme: (a) $AC=\sqrt{36+64}=10$ cm [A1]; base area $=\dfrac12\times6\times8=24$ [M1]; volume $=288$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $CD=\sqrt{10^{2}+12^{2}}=15.6$ cm [M1][A1]; angle $DCA$ with $\tan DCA=\dfrac{12}{10}$ [M1]; $50^{\circ}$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) two triangles $=48$ and three rectangles $=(6+8+10)\times12=288$ [M1]; $336$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its projection onto the plane: here $CD$ projects to $CA$.

subtopic: Cylinder with a conical cavity
statement: A solid metal cylinder has radius $6$ cm and height $10$ cm. A conical cavity is drilled out of the top: the cone has the same circular top face as the cylinder, and its apex is at the center of the bottom face. (a) Find the exact volume of metal remaining. [3] (b) Find the exact slant height of the cone. [1] (c) Find the exact total surface area of the remaining solid, including the surface of the cavity. [3]
markscheme: (a) cylinder $=\pi\times36\times10=360\pi$ [A1]; cone $=\dfrac13\pi\times36\times10=120\pi$ [A1]; remaining $=240\pi$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $\sqrt{6^{2}+10^{2}}=\sqrt{136}=2\sqrt{34}$ cm [A1] [1 mark] (c) curved surface of cylinder $=2\pi\times6\times10=120\pi$ and bottom face $=36\pi$ [A1]; inside cone surface $=\pi\times6\times2\sqrt{34}=12\sqrt{34}\,\pi$ [A1]; total $=\left(156+12\sqrt{34}\right)\pi$ cm$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The top face of the cylinder disappears completely because the cone's base covers it.

subtopic: Cone-shaped container and a cylinder
statement: A container is in the shape of a cone with the apex pointing downward, radius $6$ cm at the top and vertical height $18$ cm. It is filled with water to a depth of $9$ cm. (a) Find the radius of the water surface. [2] (b) Find the volume of water, correct to 3 significant figures, and show that it is $\dfrac18$ of the volume of the full container. [4] (c) The water is poured into an empty cylindrical glass of radius $5$ cm. Find the depth of the water in the glass, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) similar triangles [M1]; radius $=\dfrac{6\times9}{18}=3$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\dfrac13\pi\times3^{2}\times9=27\pi=84.8$ cm$^{3}$ [M1][A1]; full volume $=\dfrac13\pi\times36\times18=216\pi$ [A1]; $\dfrac{27\pi}{216\pi}=\dfrac18$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $25\pi h=27\pi$ [M1]; $h=1.08$ cm [A1] [2 marks]
tips: A similar smaller cone of half the height has half the radius and $\left(\frac12\right)^{3}$ of the volume.

subtopic: Perpendicular bisector of two sites
statement: Two sites $A(3, 1)$ and $B(9, 3)$ are used to construct a Voronoi diagram. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [4] (b) Show that the point $(5, 5)$ is on the boundary between the cells of $A$ and $B$. [2] (c) Determine which site is nearer to the point $(4, 4)$. [2]
markscheme: (a) midpoint $(6, 2)$ [A1]; gradient of $AB=\dfrac13$ [A1]; perpendicular gradient $-3$ [A1]; $y=-3x+20$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y=-3(5)+20=5$, or distances $\sqrt{20}$ and $\sqrt{20}$ [M1]; equal distances to $A$ and $B$ [AG] [2 marks] (c) $d_A=\sqrt{10}$ and $d_B=\sqrt{26}$ [M1]; site $A$ is nearer [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from both sites; compare squared distances to avoid square roots.

subtopic: Voronoi vertex of three sites
statement: Three sites are $A(0, 0)$, $B(8, 0)$ and $C(4, 6)$. Consider the Voronoi diagram for these three sites. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ and of $AC$. [4] (b) Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex. [2] (c) A fire station is to be built inside triangle $ABC$ at the point that is as far as possible from its nearest site. Find the greatest possible distance from the fire station to its nearest site. [3]
markscheme: (a) $AB$: $x=4$ [A1]; midpoint of $AC$ is $(2, 3)$ and gradient of $AC$ is $\dfrac32$ [A1]; perpendicular gradient $-\dfrac23$ [A1]; $y-3=-\dfrac23(x-2)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) substitute $x=4$ [M1]; $y=3-\dfrac43=\dfrac53$, so $\left(4, \dfrac53\right)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) the best position is the Voronoi vertex, the center of the largest empty circle [R1]; distance to $A$: $\sqrt{16+\frac{25}{9}}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{13}{3}$ units, which is also the distance to $B$ and to $C$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The vertex is the circumcenter of the three sites, equidistant from all of them. It is the center of the largest empty circle inside the triangle.

subtopic: Cell boundaries and area of a cell
statement: Three towns have coordinates, in kilometers, $A(2, 3)$, $B(9, 2)$ and $C(5, 8)$. Consider the Voronoi diagram for these towns within the region $0\le x\le12$, $0\le y\le10$. (a) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (b) The perpendicular bisector of $AC$ is $y=-0.6x+7.6$. Find the coordinates of the Voronoi vertex, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) The cell of $A$ is the quadrilateral with vertices $(0, 0)$, $\left(\dfrac{36}{7}, 0\right)$, the Voronoi vertex and $(0, 7.6)$. Find its area, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Find the percentage of the whole region that is nearer to $A$ than to $B$ or $C$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) midpoint $(5.5, 2.5)$ and gradient of $AB=-\dfrac17$ [A1]; perpendicular gradient $7$ [M1]; $y=7x-36$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) $7x-36=-0.6x+7.6$ [M1]; $(5.74, 4.16)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) shoelace formula with the unrounded vertex $\left(\dfrac{109}{19}, \dfrac{79}{19}\right)$ [M1][A1]; area $=32.5$ km$^{2}$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) region area $=120$ [A1]; $\dfrac{32.49}{120}\times100=27.1\%$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Use the shoelace formula, or split the quadrilateral into two triangles, with the vertices in order around the cell.

subtopic: Nearest-neighbor estimate of rainfall
statement: Rainfall is recorded at five stations, with coordinates in kilometers and daily rainfall in millimeters: $P_1(1, 7)$, $34$ mm; $P_2(4, 2)$, $41$ mm; $P_3(8, 8)$, $29$ mm; $P_4(10, 3)$, $38$ mm; $P_5(6, 5)$, $45$ mm. The rainfall at any other location is estimated by the rainfall at the nearest station. (a) Find the nearest station to the point $Q(7, 4)$ and state the estimated rainfall there. [3] (b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $P_5$ and $P_4$. [3] (c) Find the estimated rainfall at the point $(9, 5)$, and give one weakness of this method of estimation. [3]
markscheme: (a) distances from $Q$: $6.71$, $3.61$, $4.12$, $3.16$, $1.41$ [M1][A1]; nearest is $P_5$ so $45$ mm [A1] [3 marks] (b) midpoint $(8, 4)$ [A1]; gradient $P_5P_4=-\dfrac12$ so perpendicular gradient is $2$ [A1]; $y=2x-12$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) distance to $P_4=\sqrt5$, to $P_5=3$, to $P_3=\sqrt{10}$ [M1]; nearest is $P_4$ so $38$ mm [A1]; e.g. the estimate jumps abruptly across a cell boundary [R1] [3 marks]
tips: Compute squared distances to each site and choose the smallest; boundaries are perpendicular bisectors.

subtopic: Degrees, handshaking and an Euler trail
statement: A graph has vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ and edges $AB$, $AC$, $BC$, $BD$, $CD$, $DE$, $DF$, $EF$. (a) Write down the degree of each vertex and verify the handshaking lemma. [3] (b) Explain why the graph has no Eulerian circuit, but does have an Eulerian trail. [2] (c) Write down an Eulerian trail starting at $B$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A:2,\ B:3,\ C:3,\ D:4,\ E:2,\ F:2$ [A1]; sum of degrees $=16$ [M1]; $=2\times8$ edges [A1] [3 marks] (b) vertices $B$ and $C$ have odd degree, so there is no circuit (all degrees must be even) [R1]; exactly two odd vertices, so a trail from $B$ to $C$ exists [R1] [2 marks] (c) e.g. $B\to A\to C\to B\to D\to E\to F\to D\to C$ [M1][A1] [2 marks]
tips: A circuit needs every degree even; a trail needs exactly two odd vertices, which are its start and end.

subtopic: Adjacency matrix and walks
statement: A graph has four vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ and adjacency matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, with rows and columns in the order $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$. (a) Write down the edges of the graph and the degree of $C$. [2] (b) Find $M^{2}$. [3] (c) Find the number of walks of length $3$ from $A$ to $C$, and list them. [3]
markscheme: (a) edges $AB$, $AC$, $BC$, $CD$ [A1]; $\deg C=3$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $M^{2}=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1][A1][A1] [3 marks] (c) row $A$ of $M^{2}$ times column $C$ of $M$: $2\times1+1\times1+1\times0+1\times1$ [M1]; $4$ walks [A1]; $A\,B\,A\,C$, $A\,C\,A\,C$, $A\,C\,B\,C$, $A\,C\,D\,C$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: The $(i, j)$ entry of $M^{n}$ is the number of walks of length $n$ from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$.

subtopic: Kruskal's algorithm
statement: A weighted graph has vertices $A$ to $F$ and edges with weights: $AB=7$, $AC=4$, $BC=9$, $BD=5$, $CD=8$, $CE=12$, $DE=6$, $DF=11$, $EF=3$. (a) Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree. State the edges in the order they are added. [4] (b) Find the total weight of the minimum spanning tree. [1] (c) State how many edges any spanning tree of this graph has, and explain why the tree you found is the only minimum spanning tree. [2]
markscheme: (a) order the edges by weight and add the smallest each time, provided no cycle forms [M1]; $EF\,(3)$ and $AC\,(4)$ [A1]; $BD\,(5)$ and $DE\,(6)$ [A1]; $AB\,(7)$, which completes the tree [A1] [4 marks] (b) $3+4+5+6+7=25$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $6-1=5$ edges [A1]; all edge weights are different, so the algorithm never has a choice between equal weights [R1] [2 marks]
tips: Always add the smallest remaining edge that does not create a cycle, and stop when you have $n-1$ edges.

subtopic: Prim's algorithm
statement: A weighted graph has vertices $A$ to $F$ and edges with weights: $AB=10$, $AC=6$, $AD=12$, $BC=8$, $BE=4$, $CD=9$, $CE=13$, $DE=5$, $DF=11$, $EF=3$. (a) Use Prim's algorithm starting at $A$ to find a minimum spanning tree. State the order in which edges are added. [4] (b) Find the total weight of the tree. [1] (c) Explain why Prim's algorithm does not need to check for cycles. [2]
markscheme: (a) start at $A$: add $AC\,(6)$ [A1]; then $CB\,(8)$ [A1]; then $BE\,(4)$ and $EF\,(3)$ [A1]; then $ED\,(5)$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $6+8+4+3+5=26$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) each step adds an edge joining a vertex in the tree to one outside it [R1]; so the new vertex is not already connected and no cycle can form [R1] [2 marks]
tips: From the current tree, choose the cheapest edge that joins a tree vertex to a new vertex.

subtopic: Dijkstra's algorithm on a seven-vertex network
statement: A delivery network has vertices $A$ to $G$ and roads with lengths in kilometers: $AB=9$, $AC=5$, $BC=6$, $BD=4$, $BE=12$, $CD=13$, $CF=20$, $DE=3$, $DF=8$, $EG=7$, $FG=5$. (a) Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest distance from $A$ to $G$, and state the route. [5] (b) Find the shortest distance from $A$ to $F$ and state the route. [2] (c) The road $DE$ is closed. Find the new shortest distance from $A$ to $G$ and state the new route. [3]
markscheme: (a) labels from $A$: $C=5$, $B=9$ [M1]; $D=13$ [A1]; $E=16$, $F=21$ [A1]; $G=\min(16+7,\ 21+5)=23$ [A1]; route $A\,B\,D\,E\,G$ with length $23$ km [A1] [5 marks] (b) $D=13$ then $DF=8$ gives $21$ [A1]; route $A\,B\,D\,F$, which is shorter than $A\,C\,F$ ($25$ km) [A1] [2 marks] (c) route $A\,B\,D\,F\,G$ [M1]; $9+4+8+5=26$ km [A1]; the next best route $A\,B\,E\,G$ has length $28$ km [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Label each vertex with its shortest distance so far and update the neighbors of the vertex you finalize.

subtopic: Route inspection with an odd-vertex pairing
statement: A park has six path junctions $A$ to $F$. The paths and their lengths in meters are: $AB=8$, $AC=5$, $AF=12$, $BC=6$, $BD=9$, $CD=4$, $DE=7$, $DF=3$, $EF=10$. A ranger must walk along every path at least once, starting and finishing at the same junction. (a) Find the degree of each vertex and list the vertices of odd degree. [2] (b) Find the length of the shortest route that starts and finishes at the same junction and covers every path, stating the paths that are repeated. [5] (c) The ranger instead starts at $A$ and finishes at $F$. Find the length of the shortest route that covers every path. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A:3,\ B:3,\ C:3,\ D:4,\ E:2,\ F:3$ [A1]; odd vertices are $A$, $B$, $C$, $F$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) total length of paths $=64$ [A1]; pairings: $AB+CF=8+7=15$, $AC+BF=5+12=17$, $AF+BC=12+6=18$ [M1][A1]; minimum is $15$, repeating $AB$ and the route $C\,D\,F$ [A1]; shortest route $=64+15=79$ m [A1] [5 marks] (c) only $B$ and $C$ then need pairing [M1]; shortest path $B$ to $C$ is $BC=6$ [A1]; $64+6=70$ m [A1] [3 marks]
tips: List every pairing of odd vertices using shortest connecting paths (not necessarily direct edges), and choose the smallest total.

subtopic: Travelling salesman bounds from a distance table
statement: A technician must visit five sites $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, starting and finishing at $B$ and visiting each other site exactly once. The direct travel times in minutes between sites are: $AB=12$, $AC=29$, $AD=14$, $AE=21$, $BC=26$, $BD=20$, $BE=17$, $CD=24$, $CE=7$, $DE=18$. (a) Use the nearest neighbor algorithm starting at $B$ to find an upper bound for the shortest tour. State the tour and its length. [3] (b) Delete vertex $B$ and find a minimum spanning tree of the remaining sites. Hence find a lower bound for the shortest tour. [4] (c) Show that the tour $B\to E\to C\to D\to A\to B$ is shorter than the upper bound found in part (a), and state what this tells you about the shortest possible tour. [3]
markscheme: (a) $B\to A\,(12)$ [A1]; $A\to D\,(14)$, $D\to E\,(18)$, $E\to C\,(7)$, $C\to B\,(26)$ [A1]; tour length $77$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (b) minimum spanning tree of $A$, $C$, $D$, $E$: $CE\,(7)$, $AD\,(14)$, $DE\,(18)$ [M1][A1]; weight $39$; add the two shortest edges from $B$, $BA=12$ and $BE=17$ [M1]; lower bound $=39+29=68$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $17+7+24+14+12=74$ [A1]; $74<77$ [A1]; the shortest tour length $L$ satisfies $68\le L\le74$ [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The lower bound uses a spanning tree of the other vertices plus the two cheapest edges at the deleted vertex.

subtopic: Minimum spanning tree for a cable network
statement: A utility company will connect six villages $A$ to $F$ by laying cable along existing roads. The road lengths in kilometers are: $AB=14$, $AC=9$, $AD=21$, $BC=12$, $BD=17$, $CD=15$, $CE=8$, $DE=10$, $DF=13$, $EF=18$. Laying cable costs $4500$ dollars per kilometer. (a) Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree, listing the edges in the order they are chosen. [4] (b) Find the total length of cable and its cost in dollars. [2] (c) The road $DF$ is closed. Find the new minimum spanning tree length. [2]
markscheme: (a) smallest first: $CE\,8$, $AC\,9$, $DE\,10$ [M1][A1]; $BC\,12$ (next is $DF\,13$) [A1]; $DF\,13$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $8+9+10+12+13=52$ km [A1]; $52\times4500=234000$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (c) replace $DF\,13$ by the cheapest edge connecting $F$, which is $EF\,18$ [M1]; $52-13+18=57$ km [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Village $F$ can only be connected through $DF$ or $EF$, so closing $DF$ forces $EF$.

subtopic: Handshaking lemma and degree sequences
statement: This question is about simple graphs, with no loops and no repeated edges. (a) Find the number of edges in the complete graph $K_{7}$. [2] (b) A tree has $12$ vertices. Write down its number of edges. [1] (c) Explain why no simple graph can have five vertices of degrees $4, 3, 3, 2, 1$. [2] (d) Explain why no graph can have seven vertices that each have degree $3$. [2]
markscheme: (a) each vertex has degree $6$, so $\dfrac{7\times6}{2}$ [M1]; $21$ edges [A1] [2 marks] (b) $11$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) sum of degrees $=13$ [A1]; this is odd, but the sum of degrees is twice the number of edges [R1] [2 marks] (d) sum of degrees $=21$ [A1]; this is odd, which is impossible by the handshaking lemma [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges, so it must be even.

subtopic: Route inspection starting and finishing at different vertices
statement: A bus network has junctions $A$ to $F$ and routes with lengths in kilometers: $AB=5$, $AC=9$, $BC=7$, $BD=6$, $CE=4$, $DE=8$, $DF=10$, $EF=3$. An inspector must travel along every route at least once. (a) Find the degree of each junction and state which have odd degree. [2] (b) Find the minimum distance if the inspector must start and finish at the same junction. [4] (c) Find the minimum distance if the inspector starts at $B$ and finishes at $C$, and state which route is repeated. [3]
markscheme: (a) $A:2,\ B:3,\ C:3,\ D:3,\ E:3,\ F:2$ [A1]; odd: $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) total of all routes $=52$ [A1]; pairings: $BD+CE=6+4=10$, $BC+DE=7+8=15$, $BE+CD=11+12=23$ [M1][A1]; $52+10=62$ km [A1] [4 marks] (c) only $D$ and $E$ need pairing [M1]; shortest path $D$ to $E$ is $DE=8$ [A1]; $52+8=60$ km, repeating $DE$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: If the start and end are different odd vertices, only the other odd vertices need to be paired.

subtopic: Independent events from a union
statement: Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $P(A)=0.5$, $P(B)=0.3$ and $P(A\cup B)=0.65$. (a) Find $P(A\cap B)$. [2] (b) Determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent, giving a reason. [2] (c) Find $P(A'\cap B')$. [1] (d) Find $P(A\mid B')$. [3]
markscheme: (a) $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ [M1]; $P(A\cap B)=0.15$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $P(A)P(B)=0.5\times0.3=0.15$ [M1]; equals $P(A\cap B)$, so the events are independent [A1] [2 marks] (c) $1-0.65=0.35$ [A1] [1 mark] (d) $P(A\cap B')=0.5-0.15=0.35$ [A1]; $P(B')=0.7$ [A1]; $P(A\mid B')=\dfrac{0.35}{0.7}=0.5$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Independent events satisfy $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. $P(A'\cap B')$ is the complement of the union.

subtopic: Drawing balls without replacement
statement: A bag contains $5$ red, $4$ blue and $3$ green balls. Three balls are drawn at random, one after another, without replacement. (a) Find the probability that all three balls are red. [2] (b) Find the probability that the three balls are three different colors. [3] (c) Given that the first ball drawn is red, find the probability that at least one of the other two balls is blue. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{4}{11}\times\dfrac{3}{10}$ [M1]; $\dfrac{1}{22}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) one color each in a given order: $\dfrac{5\times4\times3}{12\times11\times10}$ [M1]; there are $3!=6$ orders [M1]; $\dfrac{6\times60}{1320}=\dfrac{3}{11}$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) after a red ball there are $4$ red, $4$ blue and $3$ green balls (11 in all) [A1]; $P(\text{no blue})=\dfrac{7\times6}{11\times10}=\dfrac{21}{55}$ [M1]; $1-\dfrac{21}{55}=\dfrac{34}{55}$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For at least one, use the complement. Remember that the pool shrinks after each draw.

subtopic: Finding the mean and standard deviation of a normal variable
statement: The mass $X$ grams of an apple is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is known that $10\%$ of apples have mass less than $40$ g and $20\%$ of apples have mass greater than $70$ g. (a) Write down the standardized values corresponding to $P(X<40)=0.1$ and $P(X<70)=0.8$. [2] (b) Find $\mu$ and $\sigma$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Using your unrounded values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$, find the probability that an apple has a mass between $50$ g and $65$ g, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Use the inverse normal function to get both $z$-values, then solve two linear equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

subtopic: Binomial model for defective items
statement: A machine produces items, each defective with probability $0.12$, independently of the others. A sample of $15$ items is taken. Let $X$ be the number of defective items in the sample. (a) Find $P(X\ge3)$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ and the standard deviation of $X$, correct to 3 significant figures where needed. [3] (c) Find the smallest sample size $n$ such that the probability of at least one defective item exceeds $0.95$. [3]
tips: For at least one, use $1-P(X=0)=1-(1-p)^{n}$ and solve the inequality with logarithms or the GDC.

subtopic: Poisson model for help-desk calls
statement: Calls to a help desk arrive at random, at an average rate of $2.1$ calls every $10$ minutes. Let $X$ be the number of calls in a $10$-minute period. (a) State the distribution of $X$ and find the probability of exactly $3$ calls in a $10$-minute period, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the probability of more than $5$ calls in a $30$-minute period, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Find the probability that three consecutive, independent $10$-minute periods each have exactly $3$ calls, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Scale the mean to the length of the interval. Independent intervals multiply.

subtopic: Symmetry of the normal distribution
