statement: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $50$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. It is given that $P(X<42)=0.2$. (a) Write down $P(X>58)$. [2] (b) Find $P(42<X<58)$. [2] (c) Find $P(X<50\mid X<58)$. [3]
tips: The normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so equal distances either side have equal tail areas.

subtopic: Discrete random variable with an unknown constant
statement: A discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution $P(X=x)=k(x+1)$ for $x=1, 2, 3, 4$, where $k$ is a constant. (a) Find the value of $k$. [2] (b) Find $E(X)$. [2] (c) Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. [3] (d) Find $P(X\ge3)$. [1]
tips: Probabilities sum to $1$; $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^{2})-[E(X)]^{2}$.

subtopic: Normal probability feeding a binomial model
statement: The mass of a packet of rice is normally distributed with mean $250$ g and standard deviation $4$ g. A packet is underweight if its mass is less than $243$ g. (a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen packet is underweight, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) An inspector takes a random sample of $20$ packets. Using the unrounded probability from part (a), find the probability that at most $2$ packets are underweight, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) A batch of $500$ packets is produced. Estimate the number of underweight packets, to the nearest whole number. [2] (d) The inspector rejects a batch if a sample of $20$ contains more than $2$ underweight packets. Find the probability that a batch is rejected, correct to 3 significant figures. [1]
tips: Use the normal distribution to get the success probability, then the binomial distribution for the sample.

subtopic: Poisson fit to goals per match
statement: This question tests whether the number of goals scored per match in a football league can be modeled by a Poisson distribution. The numbers of goals in $100$ matches were recorded, and no match had more than $5$ goals. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c}\text{Goals in a match} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5\\\hline\text{Number of matches} & 11 & 28 & 30 & 18 & 9 & 4\end{array}$$ (a) Find the mean number of goals per match. [2] (b) Using a Poisson distribution with mean $1.98$, find the expected number of matches with $0$, $1$, $2$ and $3$ goals, and with $4$ or more goals, correct to 2 decimal places. [4] (c) State suitable hypotheses for a $\chi^{2}$ goodness-of-fit test, and the number of degrees of freedom when the categories $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ and $4$ or more are used and the mean is estimated from the data. [3] (d) Observed frequencies for the five categories are $11$, $28$, $30$, $18$, $13$. Find the $\chi^{2}$ statistic and the $p$-value, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (e) State the conclusion at the $5\%$ significance level, in context. [2] (f) Explain why matches with $4$ goals and $5$ goals were combined into a single category. [1]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{0\times11+1\times28+2\times30+3\times18+4\times9+5\times4}{100}$ [M1]; $1.98$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $100\,P(X=k)$ with $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(1.98)$ [M1]; $13.81$, $27.34$ [A1]; $27.06$, $17.86$ [A1]; $4$ or more: $100-86.07=13.93$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $H_0$: goals per match follow a Poisson distribution; $H_1$: they do not [A1]; categories $=5$ [A1]; $df=5-1-1=3$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $\chi^{2}=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^{2}}{E}$ [M1]; $\chi^{2}=0.968$ [A1]; $p=0.809$ [A1] [3 marks] (e) $p>0.05$ so do not reject $H_0$ [A1]; the data are consistent with goals per match following a Poisson distribution [A1] [2 marks] (f) expected frequency of $5$ goals is less than $5$, which is too small for the test [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Combine tail categories until expected counts are at least $5$. Lose one extra degree of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data.

subtopic: Chi-squared test of independence
statement: A school asks $80$ Year 12 students and $80$ Year 13 students for their main revision method: online resources, textbook or a mixture of both. The results are in this contingency table. $$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}\text{ } & \text{Online} & \text{Textbook} & \text{Mixture}\\\hline\text{Year 12} & 34 & 22 & 24\\\text{Year 13} & 20 & 38 & 22\end{array}$$ A $\chi^{2}$ test of independence is carried out at the $5\%$ significance level. (a) State the null and alternative hypotheses. [1] (b) Find the number of degrees of freedom and the expected frequency for Year 12 students who prefer a textbook. [3] (c) Use your GDC to find the $\chi^{2}$ statistic and the $p$-value, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) State the conclusion in context, with a reason. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: revision method is independent of year group; $H_1$: revision method is not independent of year group [A1] [1 mark] (b) $df=(2-1)(3-1)=2$ [A1]; $\dfrac{80\times60}{160}$ [M1]; $30$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\chi^{2}=7.98$ [A1]; $p=0.0185$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $0.0185<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [A1]; there is evidence that revision method depends on year group [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Expected frequency is row total times column total divided by the grand total.

subtopic: Two-sample t-test comparing battery lives
statement: A company compares the lives, in minutes, of batteries from two brands. Random samples gave the following. Brand A ($9$ batteries): $312$, $298$, $325$, $301$, $318$, $290$, $309$, $322$, $305$. Brand B ($10$ batteries): $289$, $301$, $284$, $296$, $278$, $292$, $299$, $287$, $281$, $294$. Assume both populations are normally distributed with equal variances. Use a significance level of $5\%$. (a) State suitable hypotheses to test whether Brand A has a longer mean battery life than Brand B. [2] (b) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation for each brand, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Use your GDC to carry out a pooled two-sample $t$-test and find the $t$-statistic, the number of degrees of freedom and the $p$-value. [3] (d) State the conclusion of the test, in context. [2] (e) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu_A-\mu_B$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (f) State two assumptions made in this test, and explain why the confidence interval supports the conclusion. [2]
markscheme: (a) $H_0$: $\mu_A=\mu_B$ [A1]; $H_1$: $\mu_A>\mu_B$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Brand A: $\bar x=309$, $s=11.6$ [A1]; Brand B: $\bar y=290$ [A1]; $s=7.67$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) two-sample pooled $t$-test [M1]; $t=4.21$ and $df=17$ [A1]; $p=0.000296$ [A1] [3 marks] (d) $p<0.05$ so reject $H_0$ [A1]; there is sufficient evidence that Brand A batteries last longer on average [A1] [2 marks] (e) pooled two-sample interval on the GDC [M1]; $(9.37, 28.2)$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (f) normal populations and equal variances (and independent random samples) [A1]; the interval contains only positive values, so $\mu_A>\mu_B$ [R1] [2 marks]
tips: A pooled test assumes equal variances. For a one-sided test, use the one-tailed $p$-value.

subtopic: Confidence interval from a small sample
statement: The lengths, in centimeters, of eight randomly chosen bolts from a production line are $12.1$, $11.8$, $12.6$, $12.3$, $11.9$, $12.4$, $12.0$, $12.2$. The lengths are normally distributed. (a) Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (b) Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean length, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find a $99\%$ confidence interval for the population mean, correct to 3 significant figures, and explain why it is wider than the $95\%$ interval. [3] (d) Suppose the population standard deviation is known to be $0.3$ cm. Find the least sample size for a $95\%$ confidence interval with margin of error at most $0.1$ cm. [3]
markscheme: (a) $\bar x=12.2$ [A1]; $s_{n-1}=0.267$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $t$-interval with $df=7$ [M1]; $(11.9, 12.4)$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) $(11.8, 12.5)$ [A1]; a higher confidence level needs a larger critical value [R1]; hence a larger margin of error [R1] [3 marks] (d) $1.96\times\dfrac{0.3}{\sqrt n}\le0.1$ [M1]; $n\ge34.6$ [A1]; $n=35$ [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Use a $t$-interval when $\sigma$ is estimated from the sample and a $z$-interval when $\sigma$ is known.

subtopic: Courier network: shortest paths, spanning tree and inspection
statement: This question analyzes a courier network. The depot is $S$ and the customer is $T$. The roads and their lengths in kilometers are: $SA=4$, $SB=7$, $AB=2$, $AC=6$, $BC=3$, $BD=7$, $CD=5$, $CE=9$, $DE=2$, $DT=4$, $ET=3$. (a) Show that exactly two vertices have odd degree, and state them. [2] (b) Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest route from $S$ to $T$ and its length. [4] (c) Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree, listing the edges, and state its total weight. [4] (d) A road sweeper must travel along every road at least once, starting and finishing at $S$. Find the length of the shortest such route. [4] (e) A second sweeper starts at $A$ and finishes at $E$. Find the length of the shortest route covering every road, and state whether any road is repeated. [2] (f) The road $BD$ is closed. Find the new shortest route from $S$ to $T$ and its length. [3]
markscheme: (a) degrees: $S:2,\ A:3,\ B:4,\ C:4,\ D:4,\ E:3,\ T:2$ [A1]; odd vertices are $A$ and $E$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) labels $A=4$, $B=6$ [M1]; $C=9$, $D=13$ [A1]; $E=15$ and $T=\min(17, 18)=17$ [A1]; route $S\,A\,B\,D\,T$ of length $17$ km [A1] [4 marks] (c) edges in order: $AB\,(2)$, $DE\,(2)$ [M1]; $BC\,(3)$, $ET\,(3)$ [A1]; $SA\,(4)$ and $CD\,(5)$ (rejecting $DT$, which forms a cycle) [A1]; total weight $19$ km [A1] [4 marks] (d) total length of roads $=52$ [A1]; $S$ has even degree, so only $A$ and $E$ must be paired [M1]; shortest path from $A$ to $E$ is $A\,B\,D\,E=11$ [A1]; $52+11=63$ km [A1] [4 marks] (e) $A$ and $E$ are the only odd vertices, so an Eulerian trail exists [M1]; length $52$ km and no road is repeated [A1] [2 marks] (f) candidate $S\,A\,B\,C\,D\,T=4+2+3+5+4$ [M1]; $=18$ km [A1]; the alternatives $S\,A\,B\,C\,D\,E\,T$ ($19$ km) and $S\,A\,C\,D\,T$ ($19$ km) are longer [A1] [3 marks]
tips: For the sweepers, only vertices of odd degree that are not the start or end need to be paired.

subtopic: Travelling salesman: upper and lower bounds with several deleted vertices
statement: A courier must visit five towns $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$ and return to the start, visiting each other town exactly once. The direct travel times in minutes are: $AB=6$, $AC=10$, $AD=8$, $AE=16$, $BC=20$, $BD=18$, $BE=22$, $CD=11$, $CE=13$, $DE=24$. Each minute of driving costs $0.85$ dollars. (a) Use the nearest neighbor algorithm starting at $A$ to find the tour and its length. [3] (b) Delete vertex $C$. Find a minimum spanning tree of the remaining four towns and hence a lower bound for the shortest tour. [4] (c) Deleting vertex $A$ instead gives a lower bound of $56$. State the best lower bound and the interval in which the shortest tour length $L$ lies. [2] (d) Find the length of the tour $A\to B\to E\to C\to D\to A$ and state the improved upper bound. [2] (e) Find the saving in driving cost, in dollars, of using the tour in part (d) instead of the tour from part (a). [2] (f) Explain why the lower bound found by deleting a vertex cannot exceed the length of the shortest tour. [1]
markscheme: (a) $A\to B\,(6)$, $B\to D\,(18)$ [A1]; $D\to C\,(11)$, $C\to E\,(13)$ [A1]; $E\to A\,(16)$, so length $64$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (b) spanning tree of $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$: $AB\,6$, $AD\,8$, $AE\,16$ [M1][A1]; weight $30$; the two shortest edges at $C$ are $CA=10$ and $CD=11$ [M1]; lower bound $=30+21=51$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) the greater lower bound is $56$ [A1]; $56\le L\le64$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $6+22+13+11+8=60$ [A1]; upper bound $60$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (e) time saved $=64-60=4$ minutes [A1]; $4\times0.85=3.40$ dollars [A1] [2 marks] (f) removing the vertex from any tour leaves a spanning path, which is at least as long as the minimum spanning tree, and the two tour edges at the vertex are at least the two shortest edges [R1] [1 mark]
tips: A lower bound: minimum spanning tree of the remaining vertices plus the two shortest edges at the deleted vertex.

subtopic: Linear coding and adding a data value
statement: A data set of $10$ numbers $x_1, \ldots, x_{10}$ has mean $12$ and standard deviation $3$. (a) A new data set is formed by $y=2x-5$. Find the mean and the standard deviation of $y$. [3] (b) An eleventh number equal to $12$ is added to the original data set. Find the new mean and show that the new variance is $\dfrac{90}{11}$. [4] (c) Write down the exact new standard deviation. [1]
markscheme: (a) mean $=2\times12-5=19$ [A1]; standard deviation is multiplied by $|2|$ [M1]; $6$ [A1] [3 marks] (b) new mean stays $12$ since the new value equals the old mean [A1]; $\sum(x-12)^{2}=10\times3^{2}=90$ [M1]; the new value adds $0$ to this sum [A1]; variance $=\dfrac{90}{11}$ [AG] [4 marks] (c) $\sqrt{\dfrac{90}{11}}=\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{\sqrt{11}}$ [A1] [1 mark]
tips: Adding a constant changes the mean but not the spread; multiplying by $a$ multiplies the standard deviation by $|a|$.

subtopic: Estimating mean and standard deviation of grouped data
statement: The times, in minutes, taken by $50$ students to finish a quiz are grouped: $0\le t<10$: $4$; $10\le t<20$: $11$; $20\le t<30$: $18$; $30\le t<40$: $12$; $40\le t<50$: $5$. (a) Write down the midpoints of the classes and find an estimate of the mean time. [3] (b) Use your GDC to find an estimate of the population standard deviation, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (c) Find the modal class and the class containing the median. [2] (d) A student says the true mean must be exactly $25.6$ minutes. Comment. [1]
markscheme: (a) midpoints $5, 15, 25, 35, 45$ [A1]; $\dfrac{4(5)+11(15)+18(25)+12(35)+5(45)}{50}$ [M1]; $25.6$ minutes [A1] [3 marks] (b) enter midpoints and frequencies in a list [M1]; $\sigma=10.8$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (c) modal class $20\le t<30$ [A1]; median is between the $25$th and $26$th values, which lie in $20\le t<30$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) the midpoints are only an assumption about where values lie in each class, so the mean is an estimate [R1] [1 mark]
tips: For grouped data, use class midpoints and the frequencies. The result is an estimate of the true mean.

subtopic: Cumulative frequency and percentile estimates
statement: The finishing times, in minutes, of $80$ runners are: $25\le t<30$: $6$; $30\le t<35$: $14$; $35\le t<40$: $22$; $40\le t<45$: $21$; $45\le t<50$: $11$; $50\le t<60$: $6$. Assume that times are evenly spread within each class and use linear interpolation. The lower quartile, median and upper quartile are the $20$th, $40$th and $60$th values. (a) Find the cumulative frequency at each class upper bound. [2] (b) Estimate the median, the lower quartile and the upper quartile, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (c) Estimate the percentage of runners who took more than $48$ minutes, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
tips: Linear interpolation: lower bound plus the fraction of the class needed times the class width.

subtopic: Comparing two data sets with five-number summaries
statement: The numbers of customers per day at two cafés over a period of time have these five-number summaries (minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum). Café $A$: $12$, $20$, $26$, $34$, $52$. Café $B$: $10$, $18$, $21$, $26$, $41$. (a) Find the range and the interquartile range for each café. [2] (b) Use the $1.5\times$IQR rule to decide whether either maximum is an outlier. [4] (c) Compare the two cafés, referring to a typical day and to the variability. [2]
markscheme: (a) Café $A$: range $40$, IQR $14$ [A1]; Café $B$: range $31$, IQR $8$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) Café $A$: upper fence $=34+21=55$ [M1]; $52<55$, no outlier [A1]; Café $B$: upper fence $=26+12=38$ [M1]; $41>38$, so $41$ is an outlier [A1] [4 marks] (c) Café $A$ has the higher median ($26$ against $21$), so more customers on a typical day [A1]; Café $A$ has the larger IQR ($14$ against $8$), so its numbers vary more [A1] [2 marks]
tips: An outlier lies above $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$ or below $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$.

subtopic: Combined mean and standard deviation of two groups
statement: A test is taken by two classes. Class $P$ has $20$ students with mean score $62$ and standard deviation $8$. Class $Q$ has $30$ students with mean score $70$ and standard deviation $6$. Standard deviations are population standard deviations. (a) Find the mean score of all $50$ students. [2] (b) Find $\sum x^{2}$ for each class. [3] (c) Hence find the standard deviation of all $50$ scores, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Rearrange $\sigma^{2}=\frac{\sum x^{2}}{n}-\mu^{2}$ to recover $\sum x^{2}$ for each group, then combine.

subtopic: Histogram with unequal class widths
statement: This question analyzes the journey times, in minutes, of $120$ commuters, recorded in classes of unequal width: $0\le t<10$: $12$; $10\le t<20$: $30$; $20\le t<40$: $46$; $40\le t<60$: $24$; $60\le t<100$: $8$. (a) Find the frequency density of the class $20\le t<40$. [1] (b) Estimate the mean and the population standard deviation of the journey times, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Estimate the median, the lower quartile and the upper quartile, using linear interpolation and the $60$th, $30$th and $90$th values, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) The mean is greater than the median. State what this suggests about the shape of the distribution. [1] (e) Estimate the percentage of commuters whose journey took more than $50$ minutes. [2] (f) A commuter's cost is $C=0.8t+1.5$ dollars for a journey of $t$ minutes. Use your unrounded results to find the estimated mean and standard deviation of the cost, correct to 3 significant figures. [4]
markscheme: (a) $\dfrac{46}{20}=2.3$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) midpoints $5, 15, 30, 50, 80$ [A1]; mean $=\dfrac{3730}{120}=31.1$ [A1]; $\sigma=19.1$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) cumulative frequencies $12, 42, 88, 112, 120$ [A1]; $Q_1=10+\dfrac{30-12}{30}\times10=16.0$ [A1]; median $=20+\dfrac{60-42}{46}\times20=27.8$ [A1]; $Q_3=40+\dfrac{90-88}{24}\times20=41.7$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) the distribution is positively (right) skewed, with a long tail of long journeys [R1] [1 mark] (e) cumulative frequency at $50=88+\dfrac{10}{20}\times24=100$ [M1]; $\dfrac{20}{120}=16.7\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (f) mean cost $=0.8\times31.08+1.5$ [M1]; $26.4$ dollars [A1]; standard deviation $=0.8\times19.09$ [M1]; $15.3$ dollars [A1] [4 marks]
tips: Frequency density is frequency divided by class width. Use midpoints for the mean, and interpolation for the quartiles.

subtopic: Pearson correlation and linear regression with prediction
statement: A teacher records the number of hours $x$ that eight students studied for a test and their scores $y$ out of $100$: $(2, 41)$, $(3, 48)$, $(5, 52)$, $(6, 60)$, $(7, 63)$, $(9, 70)$, $(10, 72)$, $(12, 81)$. (a) Find the Pearson correlation coefficient $r$, correct to 3 significant figures, and describe the correlation. [2] (b) Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ and interpret its gradient. [3] (c) Use the line to estimate the score of a student who studies for $8$ hours. [2] (d) Explain why the line should not be used for $x=20$. [1]
markscheme: (a) $r=0.993$ [A1]; very strong positive linear correlation [A1] [2 marks] (b) $y=3.85x+34.9$ [A1][A1]; each extra hour of study is associated with about $3.85$ more marks [A1] [3 marks] (c) $3.853\times8+34.87$ [M1]; $65.7$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x=20$ is outside the range of the data, and the prediction $111.9$ exceeds the maximum score $100$ [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Regression predictions are reliable only for values within the range of the data (interpolation).

subtopic: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
statement: Two judges score seven contestants out of $100$. Judge $1$ gives $78$, $85$, $62$, $91$, $70$, $88$, $55$. Judge $2$ gives $14$, $19$, $10$, $17$, $12$, $20$, $9$ (out of $20$) to the same contestants in the same order. (a) Rank each judge's scores, with rank $1$ for the highest score. [3] (b) Find the differences $d$ in ranks and $\sum d^{2}$, and hence calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient $r_s$, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Interpret the value of $r_s$ in context. [1]
markscheme: (a) judge $1$: $4, 3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 7$ [A1]; judge $2$: $4, 2, 6, 3, 5, 1, 7$ [A1][A1] [3 marks] (b) $d=0, 1, 0, -2, 0, 1, 0$ [A1]; $\sum d^{2}=6$ [A1]; $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\times6}{7\times48}=0.893$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) strong positive association: the judges tend to rank the contestants in a similar order [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Rank both variables the same way, and use $r_s=1-\frac{6\sum d^{2}}{n(n^{2}-1)}$ when there are no tied ranks.

subtopic: Regression line through the mean point
statement: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ for a data set is $y=1.8x+4$. The mean of the $x$ values is $10$ and the correlation coefficient is $r=0.9$. (a) Find the mean of the $y$ values. [2] (b) Use the line to estimate $y$ when $x=14$. [2] (c) Write down what the sign and size of $r$ tell you about the relationship, and about how reliable the estimate in part (b) is. [2]
markscheme: (a) the regression line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$ [M1]; $\bar y=1.8\times10+4=22$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $1.8\times14+4$ [M1]; $29.2$ [A1] [2 marks] (c) strong positive linear correlation [A1]; $x=14$ is probably within the data range, so the estimate is fairly reliable [R1] [2 marks]
tips: The least-squares line always passes through the mean point $(\bar x, \bar y)$.

subtopic: Chain rule, tangent, normal and stationary point
statement: Let $f(x)=(2x-1)^{4}$. (a) Find $f'(x)$. [2] (b) Find the equation of the tangent to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=1$, in the form $y=mx+c$. [3] (c) Find the equation of the normal at the same point, in the form $ax+by+d=0$ with integer coefficients. [2] (d) Find the coordinates of the stationary point of the graph of $f$ and determine its nature. [3]
markscheme: (a) chain rule [M1]; $f'(x)=8(2x-1)^{3}$ [A1] [2 marks] (b) $f(1)=1$ and $f'(1)=8$ [A1]; $y-1=8(x-1)$ [M1]; $y=8x-7$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) gradient $-\dfrac18$ so $y-1=-\dfrac18(x-1)$ [M1]; $x+8y-9=0$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $8(2x-1)^{3}=0$ so $x=\dfrac12$ [M1]; $\left(\dfrac12, 0\right)$ [A1]; $f'$ changes from negative to positive, so it is a minimum [R1] [3 marks]
tips: The normal has gradient equal to the negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient.

subtopic: Optimizing a cylindrical can
statement: This question investigates the design of a closed cylindrical can with volume $500$ cm$^{3}$. The can has radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm. (a) Show that the total surface area is $A=2\pi r^{2}+\dfrac{1000}{r}$. [3] (b) Find $\dfrac{dA}{dr}$ and hence find the value of $r$ that gives a stationary point, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (c) Show that this value of $r$ gives a minimum, and find the minimum surface area, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (d) Show that, for this can, $h=2r$. [2] (e) Metal for the curved side costs $0.004$ dollars per cm$^{2}$ and for the top and base costs $0.007$ dollars per cm$^{2}$. Show that the cost is $C=0.014\pi r^{2}+\dfrac{4}{r}$ dollars, and find the radius that minimizes $C$, correct to 3 significant figures. [5]
tips: Use $V=\pi r^{2}h$ to eliminate $h$ before differentiating. Check the second derivative to confirm a minimum.

subtopic: Antiderivative with a condition and a definite integral
statement: A function $f$ satisfies $f'(x)=3x^{2}-4x+1$ and $f(2)=5$. (a) Find $f(x)$. [4] (b) Find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}f'(x)\,dx$. [2] (c) Solve $f'(x)=0$. [2]
tips: Do not forget the constant of integration; use the given point to find it.

subtopic: Area between a parabola and a line
statement: The graphs of $y=x^{2}+1$ and $y=5-x$ intersect at two points. (a) Find the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (b) Find the area of the region enclosed by the two graphs, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve and integrate between the intersection points.

subtopic: Volume of a vase by rotation and the trapezoidal rule
statement: A vase is modeled by rotating the region under the curve $y=1+\sqrt{x}$, for $0\le x\le9$, through $360^{\circ}$ about the $x$-axis. Here $x$ cm is the height above the base and $y$ cm is the radius of the vase at that height. (a) Write down the radius of the vase at its base and at its top. [2] (b) Show that the volume of the vase is $\dfrac{171\pi}{2}$ cm$^{3}$ and find its value correct to 3 significant figures. [5] (c) Use the trapezoidal rule with $3$ equal strips to estimate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{9}\left(1+\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}dx$, and hence an estimate of the volume, correct to 3 significant figures. [4] (d) State, with a reason, whether the trapezoidal estimate is an underestimate or an overestimate. [2] (e) Water is poured into the vase at a constant rate of $20$ cm$^{3}$ per second. Find the time to fill the vase, correct to 3 significant figures. [2]
markscheme: (a) base: $y=1$ cm [A1]; top: $y=1+3=4$ cm [A1] [2 marks] (b) $V=\pi\displaystyle\int_{0}^{9}\left(1+\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}dx$ [M1]; $=\pi\displaystyle\int_{0}^{9}\left(1+2x^{1/2}+x\right)dx$ [A1]; $=\pi\left[x+\dfrac43x^{3/2}+\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{9}$ [A1]; $=\pi(9+36+40.5)$ [A1]; $\dfrac{171\pi}{2}=269$ cm$^{3}$ [AG] [5 marks] (c) $h=3$ and values $1,\ 7.464,\ 11.899,\ 16$ [A1][A1]; $\dfrac32\left(1+2\times7.464+2\times11.899+16\right)=83.6$ [M1]; volume $\approx263$ cm$^{3}$ [A1] [4 marks] (d) underestimate [A1]; the function $\left(1+\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}$ is concave, so the chords lie below the curve [R1] [2 marks] (e) $\dfrac{85.5\pi}{20}$ [M1]; $13.4$ seconds [A1] [2 marks]
tips: For rotation about the $x$-axis, $V=\pi\int y^{2}\,dx$. A concave integrand makes the trapezoidal rule underestimate.

subtopic: Velocity and displacement from an exponential acceleration
statement: A particle moves in a straight line. Its acceleration at time $t$ seconds is $a=4e^{-0.5t}$ m s$^{-2}$ for $t\ge0$, and it starts from rest. (a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ in terms of $t$. [3] (b) Write down the limiting value of the velocity as $t\to\infty$. [1] (c) Find the time at which the velocity first reaches $7$ m s$^{-1}$, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Find the distance traveled in the first $5$ seconds, correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
tips: Integrate acceleration to get velocity and use the initial condition. Since $v\ge0$, distance equals displacement here.

subtopic: Separable differential equation with an initial condition
statement: Consider the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^{2}y$, with $y=2$ when $x=0$. (a) Solve the differential equation, giving $y$ in terms of $x$. [4] (b) Find the exact value of $y$ when $x=1$. [1] (c) State the equation of the horizontal asymptote of the solution curve as $x\to-\infty$. [2]
markscheme: (a) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{y}\,dy=\int3x^{2}\,dx$ [M1]; $\ln y=x^{3}+c$ [A1]; $y=2$ at $x=0$ so $c=\ln2$ [A1]; $y=2e^{x^{3}}$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $2e$ [A1] [1 mark] (c) $x^{3}\to-\infty$ so $e^{x^{3}}\to0$ [M1]; $y=0$ [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Separate the variables so each side involves one variable only, integrate, then use the initial condition.

subtopic: Euler's method compared with the exact solution
statement: Consider $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ with $y=1$ when $x=0$. Use Euler's method with step size $h=0.1$, and keep every value exact (no rounding) at each step. (a) Use Euler's method to estimate $y$ at $x=0.1$, $0.2$, $0.3$ and $0.4$. [4] (b) Show that $y=2e^{x}-x-1$ satisfies the differential equation and the initial condition. [3] (c) Find the exact solution at $x=0.4$ correct to 4 decimal places, and the percentage error of the Euler estimate, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Explain why Euler's method gives an underestimate here. [1]
markscheme: (a) $y_{n+1}=y_n+0.1(x_n+y_n)$ [M1]; $y(0.1)\approx1.1$ [A1]; $y(0.2)\approx1.22$ and $y(0.3)\approx1.362$ [A1]; $y(0.4)\approx1.5282$ [A1] [4 marks] (b) $y(0)=2-0-1=1$ [A1]; $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2e^{x}-1$ [M1]; $x+y=x+2e^{x}-x-1=2e^{x}-1$ [AG] [3 marks] (c) $2e^{0.4}-1.4=1.5836$ [A1]; $\dfrac{1.5836-1.5282}{1.5836}\times100=3.50\%$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) the solution is concave up ($y''=2e^{x}>0$), so each tangent line lies below the curve [R1] [1 mark]
tips: Each step uses the gradient at the start of the step: $y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n, y_n)$.

subtopic: Mixing in a single tank
statement: A tank contains $200$ liters of pure water. Brine containing $0.15$ kg of salt per liter flows in at $4$ liters per minute. The well-mixed solution flows out at $4$ liters per minute. Let $x$ kg be the mass of salt in the tank after $t$ minutes. (a) Show that $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.6-\dfrac{x}{50}$. [2] (b) Solve the differential equation with $x=0$ when $t=0$, to find $x$ in terms of $t$. [4] (c) Find the time when the mass of salt is $20$ kg, correct to 3 significant figures. [2] (d) Use Euler's method with step size $h=10$ minutes to estimate $x$ at $t=20$, and compare with the exact value from part (b) correct to 3 significant figures. [3]
markscheme: (a) rate in $=4\times0.15=0.6$ kg per minute [A1]; rate out $=4\times\dfrac{x}{200}=\dfrac{x}{50}$ [AG] [2 marks] (b) $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{30-x}=\int\dfrac{1}{50}\,dt$ [M1]; $-\ln(30-x)=\dfrac{t}{50}+c$ [A1]; $x=0$ at $t=0$ gives $c=-\ln30$ [A1]; $x=30\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)$ [A1] [4 marks] (c) $30\left(1-e^{-t/50}\right)=20$ [M1]; $t=50\ln3=54.9$ minutes [A1] [2 marks] (d) $x(10)\approx0+10(0.6)=6$ [A1]; $x(20)\approx6+10(0.6-0.12)=10.8$ [A1]; exact $=9.89$, so Euler overestimates by $0.91$ kg [A1] [3 marks]
tips: Rewrite $0.6-\frac{x}{50}$ as $\frac{30-x}{50}$ before separating the variables.

subtopic: Coupled linear system for two connected compartments
statement: This question models the amounts of a chemical, $x$ and $y$ milligrams, in two connected compartments at time $t$ hours. The amounts satisfy $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-2x+y$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=x-2y$, with $x=10$ and $y=0$ at $t=0$. (a) Write the system in the form $\dfrac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}=A\mathbf{v}$, stating $A$. [1] (b) Find the eigenvalues of $A$. [3] (c) Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue. [2] (d) Find the solution for $x$ and $y$ in terms of $t$. [4] (e) Find the maximum amount of the chemical in the second compartment and the time at which it occurs, correct to 3 significant figures. [3] (f) Use Euler's method with $h=0.1$ to estimate $x$ and $y$ at $t=0.1$. [2] (g) Describe the long-term behavior of the system and classify the equilibrium at the origin. [2]
markscheme: (a) $A=\begin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [1 mark] (b) $(-2-\lambda)^{2}-1=0$ [M1]; $\lambda^{2}+4\lambda+3=0$ [A1]; $\lambda=-1$ and $\lambda=-3$ [A1] [3 marks] (c) $\lambda=-1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1]; $\lambda=-3$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [A1] [2 marks] (d) $\mathbf{v}=\alpha e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}+\beta e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$ [M1]; $\alpha+\beta=10$ and $\alpha-\beta=0$ [A1]; $\alpha=\beta=5$ [A1]; $x=5e^{-t}+5e^{-3t}$ and $y=5e^{-t}-5e^{-3t}$ [A1] [4 marks] (e) $\dfrac{dy}{dt}=-5e^{-t}+15e^{-3t}=0$ [M1]; $e^{2t}=3$ so $t=0.549$ hours [A1]; $y=1.92$ mg [A1] [3 marks] (f) $x\approx10+0.1(-20)=8$ [A1]; $y\approx0+0.1(10)=1$ [A1] [2 marks] (g) both eigenvalues are negative, so $x,y\to0$ [A1]; the origin is a stable node [A1] [2 marks]
tips: Eigenvalues give the decay rates and the eigenvectors give the directions. Both being negative means every solution decays to the origin.
